WARRANT OF ARREST The Act of Assembly of Pennsylvania, of 12th July, 1842, 1 

Purd. 255 et seq. to abolish imprisonment for debt, and to punish fraudulent debtors, provides that no person shall be arrested or imprisoned on any civil process issuing out of any court of the Commonwealth, in any suit or proceeding instituted for the recovery of any money due upon any judgment or decree, founded upon contract, express or implied, or for the recovery of any damages for the nonperformance of any contract, excepting in proceedings as for contempt, to enforce civil remedies, actions for fines or penalties, or on promises to marry, on moneys collected by any public officer, or for any misconduct or neglect in office, or in any professional employment; in which cases the remedies remain as they were before the passage of that act. 

The said Act also provides that in all cases where the party to a suit cannot be arrested or imprisoned; that it shall be lawful for the party who shall have commenced a suit, or obtained a judgment in any court of record, to apply to any judge of the

WARRANT OF ARREST 

349 court in which the suit shall have been brought for a warrant to arrest the party against whom the suit shall have been commenced, or the judgment shall have been obtained, whereupon the said judge shall require of the said party satisfactory evidence, either by the affidavit of the party making such application or some other person or persons, that there is a debt or demand due to the party making such application from the other party in a suit or judgment, in which affidavit the nature and amount of the indebtedness shall be set forth as near as may be.

If the demand set forth in the affidavit be such that the party could not, according to the provisions of the said act, be arrested, and if the affidavit shall establish to the satisfaction of the judge, one or more of the following particulars, to wit:

That the party is about to remove any of his property out of the jurisdiction of the court on which such suit is brought, with intent to defraud his creditors. 

Or, that he has property which he fraudulently conceals: 

Or, that he has rights in action, or some interest in any public or corporate stock, money, or evidence of debt, which he unjustly refuses to apply to the payment of any such judgment or judgments, which shall have been rendered against him, belonging to the complainant:

Or, that he has assigned, removed, or disposed of, or is about to dispose of, any of his property with intent to defraud his creditors:

Or, that he fraudulently contracted the debt or incurred the obligation respecting which suit is brought. 

It shall be the duty of the said judge to issue a warrant of arrest.

It is required by said act that the above warrant shall be accompanied by a copy of all affidavits presented to the judge, upon which the warrant was issued, which shall be certified by such judge, and shall be delivered to the party at the time of serving the warrant by the officer serving the same. 

The officer to whom such warrant shall be delivered, shall execute the same by arresting the person or persons therein named, and bringing him or them before the judge issuing the warrant, and shall keep him in custody until he shall be duly discharged or committed, as provided in said act.

On the appearance of the person so arrested before the judge, he may controvert any of the facts and circumstances on which such warrant issued, and may at his option verify his allegations by his affidavit, and in case of his so verifying the same, the complainant may examine him on oath, touching any fact or circumstance material to the inquiry, and the answers on such examination shall be reduced to writing and subscribed by him, and the officer conducting such inquiry shall also receive such other proof as the parties may offer, either at the time of such first appearance or at such other times as such hearing shall be adjourned to, and in case of an adjournment, the judge may take a bond with or without surety for the appearance of the party arrested at the adjourned hearing. 

The judge can discharge or commit to the jail, as the facts in the case may appear; but such commitment shall not be granted if the defendant shall pay the debt or demand claimed with costs of suit, and of the proceedings against him, or give security to the satisfaction of the judge before whom the hearing shall be had, that the debt or demand, with the costs of suit and proceedings against him shall be paid with interest, within sixty days, if the demand be in judgment, and the length of time for stay of execution given by law on debts of like amount has expired, and if the said length of time has not elapsed, then, that the same shall be paid at the expiration of that time, if that shall be sixty days distant from the time of giving said security, and if not, then, that the same shall be paid within sixty days from the time of giving the same. If the demand be not in judgment at the time of giving said security, the day of payment shall be regulated by the same rule, but in no case shall the party be required to give surety for the payment of the debt before the recovering of judgment.

It is further provided that such commitment shall not be granted if the party arrested shall give bond to the complainant in a penalty of not less than twice the amount of the debt or demand claimed, with such sureties as shall be approved by such judge, conditioned that he will not remove any property which he then has, out of the jurisdiction of the court in which suit is brought, with the intent to defraud any of his creditors, and that he will not assign, sell, convey, or dispose of any of his property with such intent, or with a view to give a preference to any credit for any debt, antecedent to such assignment,

AFFIDAVIT FOR WARRANT 

351 sale, conveyance, or disposition, until the demand of the complainant, with costs, shall be satisfied, or until thirty days after final judgment shall be rendered in the suit brought for the recovery of such demand; provided, however, that the 10th section of said act shall apply only to cases where the only fraudulent design against the party arrested is, that he is about to remove any of his property out of the jurisdiction of the court in which such suit is brought, with intent to defraud his creditors.

The said act further provides that the commitment shall not be granted if the person arrested shall give bond with securities that he will within thirty days apply by petition to the Court of Common Pleas of the county, or a judge thereof, if not in session, for the benefit of the insolvent laws. For further provisions on this subject, see said Act of 12th July, 1842. P. L. 

339, 1 Purd. 255 et seq.

The following forms are given under this Act of 12th of July, 1842, and may be varied to suit any of the above-mentioned provisions.

DISCHARGE FROM ARREST SEE INSOLVENT;  

By provision of the Act of June 1, 1915, P. L. 704, an arrested debtor may petition for discharge from arrest setting forth his inability to pay the debt. Thereupon the court grants a rule to show cause and the defendant enters security to appear. At the hearing all books, etc., are to be produced and all questions put to the defendant are to be answered. The discharge in no way affects the defendant's liability under the judg ment.

(Signature of Defendant's Attorney.) (Date.) ASSIGNMENT SEE , ETC.; COLLATERAL SECURITY 

An assignment, in common parlance, signifies the transfer of any kind of property, real, personal, or mixed, and whether the same be in possession or in action. 

In a more technical sense, it is usually applied to the transfer of a term of years; but it is more properly used to signify a transfer of some particular estate or interest in lands. The proper technical words of an assignment are assign, transfer, and set over; but the words grant, bargain and sell or any other words which will show the intent of the parties to make a complete transfer, will amount to an assignment. Assignments of interest in real estate, and the like, should be acknowledged and recorded. Notice of an assignment of a chose in action, a legacy, etc., must be given to the debtor or party holding the fund or estate, in order to give priority over a later assignment of which notice is given. Phillips' Estate (No. 3), 205 Pa. 515. The notice should be in writing and give full details of the assignment, or enclose a copy thereof. 

For specific forms of assignment, see appropriate titles, such as GROUND RENTS; JUDGMENTS; LEASES; MORT- GAGES, etc., etc.

ASSIGNMENT FOR BENEFIT OF CREDITORS SEE DEEDS; INSOLVENTS 

Such assignments must be by deed, recorded in the Recorder's office of the county in which the assignor resides, within thirty days after the execution thereof. If not so recorded the assignment is void as against creditors. If the assignment includes land in another county, the deed should also be recorded there, in order to guard against a subsequent conveyance without notice. Where a nonresident of this state is the assignor, the assignment may be recorded in any county where the property is situated.

The wages of miners, mechanics, and laborers are preferred, to an amount not exceeding $100 each. Preference is also given, in certain cases, under the Acts of 1872 and 1883, to the wages of miners, mechanics, laborers and clerks, and other employees, not exceeding $200 each. (See 4 Purd. 5039 et seq.) Subject to these exceptions, and to the payment of liens, the proceeds of the property assigned are to be distributed among all the creditors, in proportion to their several demands. 

The assignor usually reserves property exempt from execution, but if such reservation is not inserted in the deed, he may, nevertheless, retain articles of household furniture, and things of domestic use, to the value of $300. 

It is the duty of the assignee to file in the prothonotary's office an inventory of the property assigned, within thirty days after the execution of the assignment, together with his affidavit that the same is a full and complete inventory of all estate and effects, so far as the same have come to his knowledge. The appraisers are to be appointed by the court or by a judge in vacation. When the inventory is filed, the assignee must give bond, with at least two sufficient sureties, to be approved by a judge,

DEED 

379 in double the amount of the inventory.

The Act of 1883 pre scribes the condition in the bond. The inventory must include the real estate, as well as personal property assigned. 

Provision is made by the Acts of February 17, 1876, and May 

24, 1893, (1 Purd. 1898 et seq.), for the sale of encumbered real estate, clear of liens, either at public or private sale. 

See Acts of 1917, P. L. 268; 1921, P. L. 1045.

Assignment to Amicable Trustee THIS AGREEMENT, made this between day of 

A. D. of the City of Philadelphia, State of Pennsylvania, (hereinafter called the debtor), and of the City and State aforesaid, (hereinafter called trustee).

WITNESSETH: 

WHEREAS, debtor is engaged in the business of selling at retail toys and radio supplies and kindred merchandise in the City of Philadelphia, State of Pennsylat

TO TRUSTEE 

381 vania, and has become financially embarrassed and is unable to pay his indebtedness in full, and WHEREAS, debtor's assets, if liquidated, without the necessity of Court proceedings, will save his creditors the substantial expenses thereof and the delay usually incident thereto.

Now, THEREFORE, in consideration of the foregoing and of the mutual promises hereinafter contained, the parties hereto do hereby agree, one with the other, as follows: 

1. Debtor hereby bargains, sells, conveys, assigns, transfers, sets over and delivers unto the said trustee, his successors and assigns, all and singular his assets or property of every kind or nature, wheresoever situate and in whosesoever hands the same may be, subject, however, to his claim for exemption as provided by law, as is hereinafter more particularly set forth, to have and to hold the same IN TRUST, nevertheless, upon the terms and conditions as hereinafter contained. 

2. Debtor reserves, as his lawful exemption from the sale of his said assets and property to said trustee, his wearing apparel and cash or merchandise to the value of three hundred dollars ($300.00), which said cash or merchandise will be selected by the said debtor and set apart by the said trustee as soon as convenient, but said trustee may, at his option, sell any such merchandise together with the other assets as hereinafter provided and pay to said debtor from the proceeds of said sale the sum of three hundred dollars ($300.00) in lieu thereof. 

3. Said trustee, as soon as convenient, shall sell, dispose of and liquidate all of the assets and property of said debtor either at private or public sale upon such terms and conditions and in such manner as to him may be deemed most advantageous; and he shall collect and recover all outstanding claims and debts due to the debtors. 

4. Said trustee shall forthwith prepare and forward to all creditors of the said debtor notice of the execution of

this agreement and the sale and delivery of the assets of said debtor to said trustee in pursuance thereof and shall advise said creditors of the contemplated sale of said assets and the plan of distribution of the proceeds thereof as hereinafter set forth, and shall submit to said creditors a release to be executed by said creditors in consideration of the distribution as herein provided to be executed by said creditors in full settlement and satisfaction of all claims and demands by each of them against the said debtor. 

5. As soon as the aforesaid release has been executed by all creditors, except possibly those creditors whose claims are less than ten dollars ($10.00), said trustee shall forthwith proceed to make distribution of the proceeds of said sale, after the adjustment of all disputes of any kind, as follows: (a) Federal, State and Municipal taxes. (b) The costs, expenses and charges, including reasonable compensation to the trustee and his counsel and to counsel for debtor. (c) Debtor's claim for exemption of three hundred dollars ($300.00) in cash, if the trustee exercises his option to pay the same in cash as hereinbefore set forth. (d) All claims entitled to priority, provided, however, that if there shall be insufficient assets remaining to pay such claims in full pro rata among such claimants. (e) The balance of proceeds remaining to be distributed pro rata among the general unsecured creditors. 

6. The Trustee shall have the right to agree with any creditor upon the amount and/or the order of his priority in payment and when all the said disputes shall be agreed upon the same shall be binding, final and conclusive upon all parties hereto. 

7. Said trustee shall not be chargeable or liable personally for any of his acts or omissions, or the acts or omissions of his attorneys and agents, if in good faith, and shall only be liable for wilful misfeasance or gross

PETITION FOR APPRAISERS 

383 negligence in the performance of the duties as herein provided. 

8. Debtor, for the purpose of making distribution by said trustee of the proceeds realized in the liquidation of said assets and property, hereby represents that to the best of his knowledge and belief the attached schedule "A" is a true and correct list of all his creditors with their last known address and that the amount set opposite their respective names is respectively due to each of them. 

9. Debtor hereby expressly represents that he has not been guilty of any act which would bar his discharge in bankruptcy. 

10. The undersigned hereby agrees to act as trustee of said assets and property of the debtor in accordance with the terms and conditions herein set forth. 

11. This agreement shall be binding upon the heirs, executors, adm'rs, successors and assigns of all the parties hereto.

Decree for Sale of Assigned Estate

In the Court of Common Pleas of County.

In the matter of the assigned estate of John Jones and Jane his wife. 

And now, 19—, the petition of Thomas Truman, assignee for the benefit of creditors of John Jones and Jane his wife, praying for an order to sell the assigned real estate, was presented and read. It was shown that sufficient notice of the intended presentation thereof had been given to all lien creditors, and that the assignee had given bond with security, as required by law. 

The Court, upon due consideration, deems it for the manifest interest of all parties, that said real estate be sold, and does hereby order and empower the said Thomas Truman, assignee as aforesaid, to make public sale thereof, and upon payment of the purchase-money and confirmation of the sale, to convey the same to the purchaser or purchasers. Notice of the sale to be given in accordance with the Act of Assembly. The sale to be held upon the premises. Ten per cent of the purchase money to be paid in cash on the day of sale, and the balance on or before the return day of this order. Report of the action of the assignee in execution of this order, to be made to the Court on the first day of next term. 

A stay of execution is ordered upon all liens against the said real estate that may be divested by the sale hereby authorized, until this order shall be expended or revoked.

ATTACHMENT 

An ATTACHMENT in criminal-law practice, is a writ requiring the sheriff or other proper officer, to arrest a particular person, who has been guilty of a contempt of court, and to bring the offender before the court.

An attachment in civil-law practice is a writ issued by a court of competent jurisdiction, commanding the sheriff or other proper officer to seize any property, credit, or right belonging to the defendant, in whatever hands the same may be found, to satisfy the demand which the plaintiff has against him. Bouv. 

Law Dic.

In Pennsylvania there are various forms of the Writ of Attachment in use, the principal of which are-Foreign Attachment, Domestic Attachment, Attachment of Vessels, Execution 

Attachment under the Act of 16th June, 1836, Attachment against absent and fraudulent debtors, under the Act of 12th 

July, 1842, and Act of 17th March, 1869, Attachment against 

Witness, &c.

For the various forms of Writs of Attachment and Docket Entries, before Justices of the Peace and Aldermen, see Binns's Justice.

ATTACHMENT FOREIGN ATTACHMENT 

The FOREIGN ATTACHMENT is a mode of proceeding by a creditor against the property of his debtor, when the debtor is out of the jurisdiction of the state, and is not an inhabitant of the same. The object of this process is, in the first instance, to compel an appearance by the debtor, although his property may eventually be made liable to the amount of the plaintiff's claim. 

It is issued solely for the benefit of the plaintiff. 

1. The plaintiff must be creditor of the defendant; the claim of the plaintiff need not, however, be technically a debt; but it may be such on which an action of assumpsit would lie. An attachment will also lie for the demand which arises ex delicto, for a tort committed with the commonwealth. (Act of 21st 

June, 1911, P. L. 1097, Purd. (1911) 286.) And on bill in equity against foreign defendants, where there is a prayer for a decree for the payment of money by them. 2 Purd. 1716-17. 

2. The writ may be issued against the real and personal estate of any person not residing within the commonwealth, and not being within the county in which such writ may issue, at the time of the issuing thereof, or against any corporation incorporated under the laws of any other state or territory. Act 1911, supra. And proceedings may be had against persons convicted of crime and sentenced to imprisonment. 

3. The writ is in general terms, not specifying in the body of it the name of the garnishee, or the property to be attached, but commanding the officer to attach the defendant, by all and singular his goods and chattels, in whose hands or possession soever the same may be found, in his bailiwick, so that he be and appear before the court at a certain time to answer, &c., Bouv. L. Dict. 

If the defendant does not appear the plaintiff files his statement and takes judgment at the third term after issuance of the writ, no service on the defendant of the statement is necessary. 

If the defendant appears or dissolves the attachment judgment for want of an affidavit of defense can be taken 15 days after service of the statement.

The defendant or the garnishee may dissolve the attachment by furnishing bail in double the amount of the claim and the action proceeded in as in assumpsit or trespass. 

If the garnishee appears interrogatories issue to him and judg ment accordingly. If the garnishee does not appear a scire

FOREIGN ATTACHMENT 

407 facias may issue and if no answer then judgment and execution thereon. Præcipe

(Caption.) To the Honorable Judges of the Said Court: 

The prayer of your petitioner respectfully represents, 1. That the plaintiff caused a writ of foreign attachment in trespass to be issued out of your Honorable Court on August 2, 1928, against the above named defendant, and that attachments were served on the Penn National Bank, attaching the bank account of X. Y., and on R. L., at

FOREIGN ATTACHMENT 

413 

2. That the Act of May 15th, 1874, amending the Act of June 13th, 1836, gives the right to a plaintiff to issue a writ of foreign attachment against any person who being a resident of this Commonwealth shall have removed therefrom, after having become liable in an action ex-delicto. That paragraph 2 of said Act of 1874, which may be found in Purdons Digest on page 1716, provides as follows: "But no such writ should be issued in the cases provided by this supplement, (the supplement being the act of 1874), except upon oath or affirmation, previously made by the person having such right of action, exdelicto, or by someone in his behalf, of the truth of the claim and of the facts upon which such attachment shall be founded, as well as that he verily believes that the person has removed to escape service of process to answer for such alleged tort; which oath or affirmation shall be filed of record." 

3. That the plaintiff caused this writ of foreign attachment to be issued without having filed the statement called for upon oath or affirmation as set forth in such section, and that therefore, the writ was improperly issued.

WHEREFOR, your petitioner, one of the attorneys for X. Y., and also for R. L., and who is making this petition in their absence, respectfully requests that a rule be granted on the plaintiff to show cause why the writ of attachment issued in the above case should not be quashed. (Jurat.) DECREE

DOMESTIC ATTACHMENT 

A DOMESTIC ATTACHMENT is so called because it may issue against persons who are inhabitants, have their domicile, or are domesticated here, in cases where they have been guilty of cer-

DOMESTIC ATTACHMENT 

427 tain acts of absconding, absenting, or concealment; and is, so far as respects creditors, in the nature of a commission of bankruptcy, because it is for the benefit of all the creditors, and all the property of the debtor is seized and distributed among them pro rata. And the like proceedings may be had if any debtor, not having become an inhabitant of this commonwealth, shall confine or conceal himself within the county, with intent to avoid the service of process and to defraud his creditors. See 

Acts of Assembly, 22d August, 1752, 4th December, 1807, and 

16th June, 1836. 1 Purd. 1266 et seq. 

1. It cannot be issued without oath or affirmation first made. 

2. It is for the benefit of all the defendant's creditors, and not for the benefit of the plaintiff alone. 

3. All the estate of the debtor is vested by the court in three trustees, not being creditors, who must give security for the due execution of the trust, and must make distribution among the creditors. Act of 16th June, 1836, Sects. 13, 15, 19, and 32. 

4. It can only be dissolved by satisfying the court [justice] that the parties were not liable to the attachment. 

5. The law on the subject of domestic attachments is founded altogether upon the Acts of Assembly, which contain comparatively full and precise directions for their regulation. But few decisions are to be found upon their construction.

ATTACHMENT AGAINST VESSELS 

SEE ADMIRALTY 

By the Act of 13 June, 1836, and its supplements, as amended by the Act of 24 June, 1895 (P. L. 251; 1 Purd. 366 et seq.)

ATTACHMENT 

all vessels built, repaired, fitted, furnished or equipped within this state are subject to a lien for work done or materials furnished, and supplies found or provided. This lien is given to all ship-builders, merchants, dealers, tradesmen and mechanics; and it binds the vessel for one year after the work is done or the materials or supplies are furnished. 

There are also acts allowing a lien on vessels navigating the Allegheny, Monongahela, or Ohio rivers, on behalf of employees for their wages, material men, wharfingers, and those claiming damages for breach of certain contracts. (1 Purd. 369.)

It must be carefully noted, however, that the jurisdiction conferred upon the state courts by these acts can be exercised by them only in cases which do not fall within strictly admiralty cognizance. Such causes as are within admiralty jurisdiction must be tried in the Admiralty Courts. See The Moses Taylor, 4 Wall. 411; The Lottawana, 21 Wall. 558.

The practice in this form of proceeding is similar, in many respects, to that pursued, in the Court of Admiralty, for the recovery of seamen's wages, and other debts contracted upon the high seas; and before the abolition of our State Court of 

Admiralty, upon the adoption of the Constitution of the United 

States, was precisely similar.

The whole proceedings are still, however, different from the course of the common law, except that the trial of disputed facts is by jury; these being ascertained, the decree and execution are according to the civil law.

ATTACHMENT EXECUTION 

Attachments under the Act of June 16, 1836, P. L. 767, issue against any person who hold a debt, pawn, pledge, stock or deposit of the defendant and summon him to answer. Stock held in another's name can be attached upon filing of an affidavit of ownership and a bond.

Procedure after service of the writ follows that in foreign attachment, which see.

ATTACHMENT AGAINST FRAUDULENT DEBTORS 

Attachment against fraudulent debtors may issue under the Act of March 17, 1869, and its supplements of 1887 for a debt in excess of $100, when the debtor (as verified by affidavit) has or is about to move, conceal, assign or dispose of his assets in fraud of his creditors. Bond must be filed in double the amount involved. Further proceedings are as in foreign attachment except that judgment for want of appearance may be taken against the defendant at or after the second term. *This rule should be allowed by a judge. By it, if the fund is $300, or less, the defendant can obtain it all, without the deduction of a counsel fee for the garnishee.

ATTESTATION 

ATTESTATION is a brief certificate annexed by the witness to an instrument vouching its execution. 

Ordinary Form of Attestation 

Signed, sealed, and delivered, in the presence of us.

Where There Are Interlineations in Instruments of Writing 

Signed, sealed, and delivered, in presence of us (the words "and his heirs and assigns" [or whatever they may be] having been previously interlined in the tenth and eighteenth lines from top of second page).

AUDITA QUERELA Where There Are Erasures and Interlineations 

Signed, sealed, and delivered, in presence of us (the words " "having been previously stricken out of the tenth line, and the words " "interlined in the same).

Attestation of an Instrument Executed by a Blind Person The above-written instrument was signed, sealed and delivered by the above-named John Jones, and he being blind, the same was carefully, truly and deliberately read over to him, in presence of us. 

Attestation for a Will

Signed, sealed, published, and declared by the abovenamed John Jones, as and for his last will and testament, in the presence of us, who, at his request, have hereunto subscribed our names at witnesses thereto, in the presence of the said testator, and of each other. 

Attestation of a Codicil 

Signed, sealed and delivered by the said A. B., as and for a codicil to be added to and considered as a part of his last will and testament, in the presence of us, who have at his request hereunto subscribed our names in the presence of the said testator and of each other.

BAILMENT LEASES 

(See Conditional Sales, Chattel Mortgage, Bills of Sale)

It needs no citation of authority to assure the bar of Pennsylvania of the favored part that the bailment lease has played

460 

BAILMENT LEASES 

in the law. Never having been interfered with by the legislature, there has been thrown around this type of agreement a network of court decisions which have given the lessor rights unheard of in any other system of law. The validity of the bailment lease extends to creditors, heirs, nominees, purchasers and bankrupt estates and is taken priority over only by landlord's distraints for rent. Even since the Conditional Sales Acts (12 

May, 1925, P. L. 603, and 1927, P. L. 979) the bailment lease is still the last word in protection to the lessor or owner (see the recent case of Stern & Co. v. Paul, 96 Super. Ct. 112, 1929.)

Lease of Chattels, Such as Furniture, Sewing Machines, Etc.

60. Petition for Compensation by Counsel for Creditors and for Trustee

To the Honorable Referee: 

The petition of L., W. & B., respectfully represents: 

1. That your petitioners, representing certain creditors, on their behalf filed an involuntary petition in bankruptcy against the above named bankrupts, on August 6, 1921. 

2. That prior thereto, to wit: on the 9 day of 1921, upon a bill in equity, a receiver was ap pointed in Common Pleas Court No. 

of the 

County of Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, as of March Term,

No. 

to take over the business of the defendants in the said bill and the bankrupts in the above cause; and the receiver thereupon appointed promptly proceeded to take charge of the said business and to liquidate the assets thereof. 9 

3. That your petitioners represented more than fifty per cent (50%) of all the creditors of the defendants in the said bill in equity, and of the bankrupts in the above cause; and in that capacity proceeded to meet with the receiver in the said equity proceedings, and to confer with him regarding the disposition of the assets of the defendants, and the payment thereout of the claims of creditors. A number of conferences were held from time to time, at which your petitioners took a leading part, as representatives of the creditors. 

4. As a result of the said conferences, it was deemed advisable that a general investigation be had of all the affairs and transactions of the defendants and bankrupts, and that it be determined to the best interests of the creditors what the exact valuation of the assets and the worth of the defendants and bankrupts were. 

5. Your petitioners then proceeded to instigate the said investigation, and had their accountants thoroughly investigate the books of the X. Y. Company. A thorough investigation thereof showed certain unfair practices that

BANKRUPTCY 

had been carried on by the defendants, and showed that the assets thereon set up were untrue and numerous other defects were found by your petitioners and their accountants. 

6. The said investigation showed that the defendants had been in the practice of selling goods in great quantities for cash, irrespective of the cost price, and numerous instances were found where merchandise had been sold for slightly more than half the original purchase price, payment to the factory having been made by long-time notes, while the company sold strictly for cash. 

7. Said investigation further showed that the cash realized in this way was not deposited to the account of the company, although they seem to have been entered in the cash books. It was further found that in order to balance the said books on the credit side of the cash books, counter entries had been falsely made, charging sums of $and in one case $to various expense, all of which were not substantiated by any invoices. 

8. Investigation further showed that the greater part of the worth-while accounts receivable had been assigned to the F. Company of America, and that among the unassigned accounts, there was on the books the account of the A. B. Company, in the sum of $- the affairs of which concern were in the hands of a receiver. 

9. Your petitioners' investigation further showed a very unsound practice on the behalf of the defendants, which was the dealing in a large note business, which was quite involved in a maze of transactions. Among the notes receivable appeared the notes of the A. B. Company, herein referred to, in the sum of $ 10. This and later investigations were taken up by your petitioners, devoting weeks at a time for the searching out of these matters. 

11. On the 6th day of August, 1921, your petitioners filed a petition in bankruptcy in the above cause, and 777

COMPENSATION 

543 thereupon on October 25, 1922, an adjudication was had. 

Your petitioners then entered into negotiations with the receiver in equity, in order that the assets which had been collected by him not be dissipated in a double receivership, or in the handling of the matter between two parties; and on December 13, 1922, at the meeting before the referee, called for that purpose, they, on behalf of the majority of the creditors, elected M. N., trustee, he having been the receiver in the equity proceedings. Your petitioners then were retained to represent the trustee in this cause, and proceeded to make a further investigation of all matters concerned therewith, and to prepare an account on behalf of the trustee, which same was filed and approved on December 28, 1922. 

12. The petitioners then investigated all the proofs that had been filed by the numerous creditors, and compared them with the books of the Company and the schedules filed. On behalf of the trustee, they then took objection to numerous of the claims which did not agree with the books and schedules, and took great pains in the reaching of reasonable stipulations with regard to the claims which had not filed any excessive amounts. They also, at the same took up the matter of petitions for reclamation filed by a number of the creditors against the bankrupts. 

13. Further investigations were then carried on into all collateral matters concerned with the bankrupts, and to obtain information from numerous outside sources. 

In connection therewith, it became necessary to examine and analyze the audits and reports of Z. Company, certified public accountants. 

14. BILLS AND NOTES See COLLATERAL SECURITY, for forms of collateral notes. 

The subject of negotiable instruments is now governed by the Act of 16th May, 1901, P. L. 194, 3 Purd. 3252 et seq., which see. 

A BILL OF EXCHANGE is defined to be an open letter of request from, and order by, one person on another, to pay a sum of

money therein mentioned to a third person, on demand, or at a future time therein specified. The first party to a bill of exchange is the drawer, or he who makes the order. The drawee is the person to whom it is addressed. The acceptor is he who accepts the bill. The payee is the party to whom, or in whose favor, the bill is made. The endorser is he who writes his name on the back of a bill. The endorsee is one to whom a bill is transferred by endorsement; and the holder is, in general, any one of the parties who is in possession of the bill and entitled to receive the money therein mentioned. 

Bills of exchange are either foreign or inland. All bills which are or purport to be both drawn and payable within the state. are inland bills. All other are foreign. Inland bills of exchange are usually denominated drafts, while the term bills of exchange is applied, in commercial parlance, to bills drawn on foreign countries.

Foreign bills of exchange consist, generally, of several parts. 

A party who has engaged to deliver a foreign bill, is bound to deliver as many parts as may be requested. The several parts of a bill of exchange are called a set; each part should contain a condition that it shall be paid, provided the others remain unpaid. The whole set make but one bill. 

There is no precise form of words necessary to a bill of exchange; but to make it negotiable, the power to assign must appear on the face of the instrument; and therefore, a bill drawn payable to A, without the words "or order," "or bearer," is not endorsable over, so as to subject the acceptor to a suit by the endorsee.

The acceptance of a bill of exchange, draft or order must be in writing and signed by the acceptor, or his lawful agent. See 

Act 1901, P. L. 194, Sec. 132.

A PROMISSORY NOTE is defined to be a promise or engagement in writing, to pay a specified sum at a time therein limited, or on demand, or at sight, to a person therein named, or his order, or to the bearer.

The person who makes the note is called the maker, the person to whom it is payable the payee, and the person to whom he transfers the instrument by endorsement the endorsee. 

Promissory notes are negotiable, and when expressed to be "without defalcation," or "without set-off," the endorsee who

takes them without notice of defense and before maturity, will not be affected by want of consideration. They may be payable in money, or in a particular kind of current money, or when payable out of the state, with current rate of exchange added: and waiver of exemption law does not destroy negotiability. Nor is negotiability destroyed by provisions authorizing the sale of collateral or confession of judgment. But generally negotiable paper must be simple, certain, unconditional, and not subject to any contingency.

Bills and notes falling due on Sundays, holidays or half holidays, are due on the next secular business day. They are not to be protested on any Saturday, but on the next business day thereafter. Act 1921, P. L. 73, No. 42. 

The following days are holidays, viz: New Year's Day, Lin coln's Birthday (February 12), Washington's Birthday (Feb ruary 22), Good Friday, Memorial Day (May 30), the Fourth of 

July, Labor Day (first Monday in September), Columbus Day 

(October 12), Election Day, Armistice Day (November 11), Christmas Day, and any day appointed or recommended by the President or the Governor as a day of thanksgiving or fasting. 

All Saturdays are half holidays after 12 o'clock noon. When 

New Year's Day, Lincoln's Birthday, Washington's Birthday, Memorial Day, the Fourth of July, Columbus Day, or Christmas 

Day falls on Sunday, the following Monday is a holiday. Act 

1921, P. L. 73, No. 42.

If a seal is added to a promissory note, it is not barred by the Statute of Limitations, which prevents the recovery of a simple contract debt, unless suit be brought, or a fresh promise of payment be made, within six years. A promissory note with a seal attached may now be transferred by a simple endorsement. Act 1901, § 6, 3 Purd. 3255.

A JUDGMENT NOTE differs from a common promissory note in having a seal appended with a power of attorney to confess judgment. The maker by the power of attorney, authorizes the payee, or his assigns, to have judgment entered, at any time, against said maker, which is a lien upon his lands, and authorizes the issuing of an execution, whenever said note shall become due and remains unpaid, without resort to a suit to obtain judgment by the ordinary course of law. Judgment notes are now negotiable: Act 1901, § 5, 3 Purd. 3254; but not if they authorize the entry of judgment at any term, whether due or not. 25 Pa. Super. Ct. 494. - day of

A PRODUCE NOTE is a written engagement to deliver, at a certain place and time, or on demand, specific articles of merchandise, merchandise of a certain general description, at current rates and to a specified value. Such notes, like due bills, are assignable, but not by mere endorsement. 

For assignment, with or without liability, the foregoing are suitable; or the following, which is somewhat shorter, will answer: "For value received, I assign the within note, with [or without] recourse, this day of 

"

In an action upon a note for the payment of a certain sum in specific articles, and at a certain place, it is not necessary for the maintenance of plaintiff's action that he should have made a demand of the articles at the time and place; but to defeat the plaintiff's action, the defendant must prove that he was ready at the time and place, and continued ready to deliver said articles. On the failure to make this proof, the plaintiff may recover the amount in money.

PROTEST 

On this subject, see the Negotiable Instruments Act of 

1901, 3 Purd. 3252 et seq. 

1. A PROTEST OF A BILL OF EXCHANGE or PROMISSORY NOTE is a formal declaration made by a Notary Public, at the request of the payee or holder, for the nonpayment of said promissory note, or for the nonacceptance or nonpayment of said bill, protesting that the drawer and all other parties to said promissory note or bill will be held responsible for the exchange, charges, damages, and interest.

Notice of protest should be forwarded to the maker or drawer, and to each of the endorsers.

A party receiving notice of protest is bound to notify those who stand prior to him on the bill, or he loses their security. 

But notice coming from any party to a bill (or his agent, as for instance a notary), will enure to the benefit of every party and operate as a notice from each endorser. 

Protest of a promissory note is not necessary; but notice of nonpayment is necessary to hold the endorsers. 

A foreign bill, appearing to be such on its face, must be protested for nonacceptance and for nonpayment. A bill not ap-

PROTEST 

573 pearing to be a foreign bill need not be protested. Act 1901, § 152, 3 Purd. 3309.

A third person may, after a bill has been protested for nonacceptance, accept it for the honor of the drawer or of any particular endorser. Such acceptance is termed an acceptance supra protest. The acceptor subjects himself to the same obligations as if the bill had been directed to him; but he can recover against the person for whom he accepts and against all who stand prior to him on the bill. 

The following precedents refer to decisions in the courts of Pennsylvania on the more important points of the subject. 

A demand of payment of the drawer, or due diligence in endeavoring to make a demand, is necessary to charge the endorser. 

But if the maker has absconded and is not to be found when the note falls due, a demand of payment is not necessary in order to charge the endorser.

Notice of the dishonor of a bill or note must be given in a reasonable time, and by not giving it the holder takes the loss upon himself.

It is settled, that whether or not due diligence was used in making inquiry for the endorser is a mixed question of law and fact. The Court are to give their opinion on the law to the jury according to the circumstances as they appear, but the jury must decide the fact whether there was due diligence or not. 

Putting a letter in the post office will be considered as notice, whether it be received or not, provided it might have reached the person to be affected, in the regular course of mail, but it will be notice only from the time at which it ought to be received. 

Protest of Bill of Exchange for Nonacceptance [or 

Nonpayment]

UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 

Here insert copy of the Bill of Exchange, with the names of the endorsers appended to said copy.

Be it known, that on the day of the date hereof, at the request of G. H., the holder of the original Bill of Exchange, of which a true copy is above written, I, the undersigned, a notary public for the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, by lawful authority duly commissioned and sworn, residing in - --, during the usual hours of

business for such purposes, presented the same at the place of business, specifying it, [or residence, specifying it, if the party be not engaged in business], of C. D., the drawee [if presented for acceptance, or "the acceptor,' if presented for payment], thereof, to the said C. BILLS OF SALE SEE BAILMENT LEASES, CONDITIONAL SALES. 

A BILL OF SALE is an agreement in writing, under seal, by which a person passes the right or interest he has in goods and chattels. 

As the law imports a consideration when an agreement is made by deed (or seal), a bill of sale, where the property is duly delivered, effects a change of ownership; but a bill of sale is not considered good against creditors where the personal property is retained in the possession of the original owner.

BONDS See ; ATTACHMENT; DECEDENTS' ESTATES; ; FIDUCIARIES; MARRIAGE; 

MORTGAGES; REPLEVIN; SURETY. And see appropriate titles such as SHERIFFS, for bonds of various officers. 

A bond or obligation is a deed whereby the obligor obliges himself, his heirs, executors, and administrators, to pay a certain sum of money to another at a day appointed. If this be all, the bond is called a single bond; but there is generally a condition added, that if the obligor does some particular act, the obligation shall be void, or else shall remain in full force and virtue. 2 Bl. Com. 340. The penal sum in a bond is usually double the amount of the real debt, and is designed to cover the amount of said debt, together with interest and costs. 

A bond, in Pennsylvania, may be transferred under Act of Assembly, by endorsement under hand and seal, in the presence of two witnesses; and in such case the assignee may bring suit in his name.

BONDS 

587 The assignee of a bond takes it at his own peril. He stands in the same place as the obligee, so as to let in every defalcation which the obligor had against the obligee at the time of the assignment or notice of the assignment, the only intent of the act being to enable the assignee to sue in his own name, and prevent the obligee from releasing after assignment. If the assignee, when he is about to take the assignment, calls upon the obligor to know whether the whole money is due, and the obligor tells him it is a good bond, but is entirely silent as to any claim of his against the bond, he can never after open his mouth against the demand of the assignee. 

Where there is a penal bond with several payments at different times, and the obligor fails to meet any one payment as it becomes due, the obligee can declare on the penalty, and take a judgment on the whole of the real debt mentioned in the bond, with stay of execution on the several payments, until such payment should become due, as by the conditions of the bond. 

Note should be made of the recent act of 1927, P. L. 985, No. 

475 known as the Uniform Written Obligations Act, providing that: "a written release or promise hereafter made and signed by the person releasing or promising, shall not be invalid or unenforceable for lack of consideration, if the writing also contains an additional express statement, in any form of language, that the signer intends to be legally bound."

Whereas, the Employer has delivered to the

Indemnity Company, a corporation of the State of hereinafter called the "Surety," certain statements in writing relative to the Employee his conduct, duties, employment and accounts, the manner of conducting the business of the employer and other things connected with the issuance of this bond, which, together with any other statements in writing hereafter made by the employer to the surety relating to any such matters, do and shall constitute the basis and form part of this contract, or any continuation or continuations thereof, and shall be warranties, it being hereby agreed, if the employer be a corporation, that any such statements made in writing by any officer or director of the corporation shall be deemed the statements of the Employer within the meaning hereof.

609 Now, THEREFORE, in consideration of the sum of dollars, paid as a premium for the period from to at 12 o'clock noon, and upon the faith of said warranties of said employer as of aforesaid, IT IS HERE- BY AGREED, that, subject to the obligations imposed by this bond on the employer, the performance of which shall be a condition precedent to the right on the part of the employer to recover under this bond, the surety shall, at the expiration of three months next after the surety, shall receive notice of default, reimburse the employer, to the extent of the sum of dollars for such pecuniary loss as the employer shall have sustained of money, securities or other personal property belonging to the employer or in the employer's possession, and for which the employer may be legally liable, caused by any act of larcency or embezzlement upon the part of the employee in the performance of the office or position in the service of the employer hereinbefore referred to, as such duties have been, or may hereafter be stated in writing by the employer to the surety, and occuring during the continuance of this bond, and discovered at any time within six months after the expiration or cancellation of this bond, or in case of the death, resignation or removal of the employee prior to the expiration or cancellation of the bond within six months after such death, resignation or removal. 

The amount of the suretyship hereunder may be increased or decreased, for separate periods, (by rider attached hereto), and this bond may be continued from year to year, at the same or an agreed premium rate so long as the surety shall consent to receive the same, in which event the surety shall remain liable under the terms hereof, between the original date of this bond and the date to which it shall have been continued: PROVIDED, that the aggregate liability of the surety for all defaults of such employee occuring during two or more periods shall not exceed a sum equal to the largest amount of suretyship in force as to such employee during any period within which 20

BONDS 

any such default shall have occurred; nor shall it be liable under the suretyship granted for any period, for defaults occuring within some other period. 

That the employer, on becoming aware of any such act which may be made the basis of any claim hereunder, shall, as soon as possible, give the surety notice thereof in writing, by a registered letter, address to the Indemnity Company, Newark, N. J., and shall, within ninety days after so becoming aware of such act as aforesaid, file with the surety claim hereunder, at the employer's own cost and expense, with full particulars thereof, duly itemized and sworn to; and, if required, the employer shall also produce in support thereof for investigation by the surety or its representative, at the office of the employer, all appropriate books, vouchers and evidence as may be required by the surety; Provided, that no claim shall be payable hereunder that shall be filed with the surety after the period of six months from the expiration or cancellation of this bond, or after a period of six months from the death, resignation or removal of the employee occurring prior to the expiration or cancellation of this bond. Provided further, that there shall be no liability on this bond for any act of larceny or embezzlement committed by the employee after the employer's first becoming aware of any act which may be made the basis of a claim hereunder. 

That if the employer shall at any time hold concurrently with this bond or represent to the surety in any statement to it, that he does or will at any time hold concurrently with this bond any other bond or guarantee of security from or on behalf of the employee, the employer shall be entitled, in the event of loss as the amount stated to claim hereunder only such proportion of the loss as the amount covered by this bond bears to the whole amount of security carried, or so stated as carried, or to be carried on the employee's behalf, whether the employer shall be able to reimburse himself from such other bond

BUILDING AND LOAN ASSOCIATIONS See MORTGAGES 

A building and loan association is a private corporation for profit. The members subscribe to the stock of the corporation and contract to pay for it in installments. The money thus accumulated is invested by the association by loaning it to the members at interest and sometimes with a premium. The loan may be a "stock loan" which is a loan where the borrowing member assigns his stock in the association as security, or it may be a "mortgage loan" which is a loan where the borrower gives a mortgage on real estate as security and subscribes to the stock of the association which is also assigned as security. 

In the latter instance, the par value of stock subscribed to must be at least the same amount as the loan. 

A stockholder may withdraw voluntarily, in which case he receives in addition to what he has paid in, such proportion of the profits of the association or such rate of interest as may be prescribed by the By-Laws. The By-Laws may provide for involuntary withdrawal and cancellation at or before maturity of the stock, provided that not less than legal interest shall be credited and allowed to each share so withdrawn and cancelled. 

See the Acts of April 29, 1874, P. L. 73; April 10, -1879, P. L. 16; April 5, 1927, P. L. 110; April 8, 1927, P. L. 179; 

April 27, 1927, P. L. 404; April 25, 1929, P. L. 766; April 16, 1929, P. L. 527; April 30, 1929, P. L. 901.

CASE STATED SEE DECLARATORY JUDGMENTS. 

The "CASE STATED" is an agreement in writing between a plaintiff and defendant, that the facts in dispute between them are true as therein stated. The facts being thus agreed upon, it is left for the court to decide in favor of which party is the law. 

As no writ of error lies on a judgment rendered on a case stated, it is usual in the agreement to insert a clause, that the case stated shall be considered in the nature of a special verdict, or to agree expressly that either party may sue out a writ of error. 91 Super. 416.

A case stated must be in a suit actually brought, and it must show a real dispute, not merely a colorable one to obtain an opinion from the court.

Despite the recent passage of the Declaratory Judgments Act of 1923, P. L. 840 (constitutional, see 284 Pa. 455), the old method of litigation by case stated is still resorted to and found useful. The decided cases should be referred to in such a proceeding (see 86 Super. 256).

CERTIFICATES 

627 

CERTIFICATES 

A CERTIFICATE is a copy of the record of a Court, duly authenticated; or a writing by which a public officer or other person bears testimony that a certain fact has or has not taken place. 

1 Greenleaf on Ev. 498.

There are two kinds of Certificates: those required by law, and those which are merely voluntary. Of the certificates required by law, are those given to an insolvent of his discharge, and those given to aliens that they have been naturalized. Voluntary certificates are those which are not required by law, but which are given of the mere motion of the party. The former are evidence of the facts therein mentioned; while the latter, which are not unfrequently extorted from weakness or ignorance, are not entitled to any credit, because the facts certified may be proved in the usual way, under the solemnity of an oath or affirmation. 2 Com. Dig. 306; Greenl. Ev. 498.

By the first section of the Act of Congress of the United States, passed March 27, 1804, "All records and exemplifications of office books, which are kept in any public office of any State, not appertaining to a court, shall be proved or admitted in any other court or office in any other state, by the attestation of the keeper of the said records or books, and the seal of his office thereto annexed, if there be a seal, together with a certificate of the Presiding Justice of the court of the county or district, as the case may be, in which such office is or may be kept; or of the 

Governor, the Secretary of State, the Chancellor, or the Keeper of the Great Seal of the State, that the said attestation is given in due form and by the proper officer; and the said certificate, if given by the Presiding Justice of a court, shall be further authenticated by the Clerk or Prothonotary of the said court who shall certify under his hand and the seal of his office that the said Presiding Justice is duly commissioned and qualified; or if the said certificate be given by the Governor, the Secretary of State, the Chancellor, or the Keeper of the Great Seal, it shall be under the great seal of the state in which the said certificate is made. And the said records and exemplifications, authenticated as aforesaid, shall have faith and credit given to them in every court and office within the United States, as they

CERTIFICATES 

have by law or usage in the courts or offices of the state from whence the same are or shall be taken.' ""

The second section provides that the first section, above recited, and the Act of 1790, shall apply to books, records, offices, &c., of the territories of the United States, and countries subject to the jurisdiction of the United States. 

By the Act of Congress of 1790, the acts of the legislatures of the several states shall be authenticated by having the seals of their respective states affixed thereto. The records and judicial proceedings of the courts of any state shall be proved by the attestation of the clerk and the seal of the court annexed, if there be a seal, together with the certificate of the Judge, Chief Justice, or Presiding Magistrate, as the case may be, that the said attestation is in due form. Revised Statutes, Sects. 905, 906. 

The certificate of a Notary Public of the dishonor of a bill or note, is evidence of the fact therein stated. Wharton on Evidence, Sect. 123; 3 Purd. 3327.

CERTIORARI 

631 

CERTIORARI 

See , as to certiorari from Supreme or 

Superior Court.

A CERTIORARI is a writ issued from a superior court directed to one of inferior jurisdiction, commanding the latter to certify to the former the record in the particular case. 

By the common law, a supreme court has power to review the proceedings of all inferior tribunals, and to pass upon their jurisdiction and decisions on questions of law. But in general the determinations of such inferior courts on questions of fact are conclusive, and cannot be reversed on certiorari, unless some statute confers the power on such supreme court. 6 Wend. 564; 

10 Pick. 358; 4 Halst. 209. When any error has occurred in the proceedings of the court below, different from the course of the common law, in any stage of the cause, either civil or criminal, the writ of certiorari is the only remedy to correct such error, unless some other statutory remedy has been given. 5 Binn. 

270; 2 Greenl. 165; 8 Ibid. 293. A certiorari, for example, is a correct process to remove the proceedings of Court of Sessions, or of County Commissioners, in laying out highways. 

Sometimes the Writ of Certiorari is used as an auxiliary process in order to obtain a full return to some other process. 

When, for example, the record of an inferior court is brought before a superior court by appeal, writ of error, or other lawful mode, and there is a manifest defect, or a suggestion of diminution, a certiorari is awarded requiring a perfect transcript and all papers.

A certiorari cannot be issued from the Supreme Court to a Justice of the Peace in a civil suit. In such case the writ must issue from the Common Pleas. Act 1810; 2 Purd. 1451.

A party or his agent or attorney, applying for a certiorari to a justice of the peace, must make affidavit that it is not intended for delay, &c. The writ must issue within twenty days after entry of judgment, unless it be in a case where the justice had no jurisdiction, or where the summons was not served and the defendant did not appear. It must be served within five days, and it is the duty of the party suing it out to serve it and to see that it is duly returned.

CERTIORARI 

An appeal and a certiorari cannot both be sustained in the same case. A losing party may choose which remedy he will pursue, but he cannot have both.

Answer Answer of the defendant county, through its county commissioners.

It is denied that the said plaintiffs have a legal, just and equitable claim for a large sum of money against the county of

It is denied that a strong local prejudice exists against the claim of the plaintiffs, and that the inhabitants of said county, as taxpayers, are prejudiced against the claim of the plaintiffs, and that a fair trial cannot be had in said county. 2 On the contrary, there is no sentiment whatever among the inhabitants and taxpayers of the said county con-

AFFIDAVITS 

637 cerning the claim of the plaintiffs. There has been no public discussion of the claim and no opportunity for prejudice to arise against the claim among the taxpayers of the county. In all the history of litigation against the said county or the municipalities thereof, it has never been the case that local prejudice has existed in favor of the county or the municipality thereof involved and against the claimant bringing suit. On the contrary, it has always been possible to secure a fair and impartial trial in all such cases.

Wherefore affiants pray the Court to dismiss the said petition [or, to discharge the said rule] at the costs of the petitioner.

CHATTEL MORTGAGES SEE BAILMENT LEASES; CONDITIONAL SALES 

CHATTEL MORTGAGES have been given very little countenance in Pennsylvania due particularly to the popularity and extensive use of the Bailment Lease. The legislature has provided however for the use of such defeasible conveyances in certain cases: (1) by lessee of coal lands or of coal mining rights in Schuylkill 

County, Act of 1853, P. L. 295; (2) lateral railroads, 1863 P. L. 

532; (3) leaseholds of collieries and manufacturing lands, 1855 

P. L. 368; (4) iron ore, its products and kindred manufactures, 1891 P. L. 102. All such mortgages must be recorded, notice thereof given and under the Act of 1887 shall be valid for only three months unless a statement of the amount due thereon be recorded in that time.

Forms are also appended applicable to mortgages to be used in other states for the convenience of Pennsylvania attorneys.

COGNOVIT ACTIONEM. 

SEE JUDGMENTS; AMICABLE ACTIONS. 

A COGNOVIT is a written acknowledgment by the defendantsubscribed but not sealed-confessing that the plaintiff's cause of action is just and true; and authorizing the plaintiff to sign judgment and issue execution for a specified sum. Sometimes the defendant confesses a part of the plaintiff's alleged claim, and denies the rest. (Caption.) 

Cognovit in Assumpsit

I confess this action, and that the plaintiff hath [or, I confess that I owe to the above-mentioned plaintiff dollars, part of the debt by him in his statement in this

COGNOVIT ACTIONEM 

651 action demanded; and that he hath] sustained damages to the amount of dollars, besides his costs and charges, in his behalf, to be taxed by the Prothonotary. 

And in case I shall make default in the payment of the sum of dollars (being the debt in this action), [or if only a part of the claim be admitted, (being so much of said claim as is admitted),] together with the said costs, on the next, the plaintiff shall be at liberty to enter up judgment for the said sum of dollars and costs as aforesaid, and sue out execution thereon for the same, together with the amount of official fees, sheriff's poundage, costs of levying, and all other incidental expenses. day of

And I do hereby agree to withdraw the plea by me pleaded to this action, and undertake not to bring any writ of error in this cause, or do any other matter or thing whereby the plaintiff may be delayed in entering judgment, and suing out execution upon default made as aforesaid.

COMPLAINT 

Complaint, in criminal law, is the allegation made to a proper officer that some person, whether known or unknown, has been guilty of a designated offense, with an offer to prove the fact, and a request that the offender may be punished.

Although peace-officers are bound, by virtue of their office, to pursue and arrest all persons suspected of crime, with or without a warrant, yet the usual practice is for some one who knows or suspects that another has been guilty of an offense against the common weal, to go to a magistrate, and there lodge his complaint, stating the grounds on which his application is made. 

It should be made on oath or affirmation, and reduced to writing by the magistrate, observing the following directions: It should be correctly dated; contain the name of the place where it is taken, the name and style of the informer, the name of the magistrate and, if possible, of the offender; the time of committing the offense, a clear description of it, and the place where it was committed. Upon this the magistrate may issue his warrant or summons, directed to the proper officer, or to any private person by name.

COMPOSITION AND EXTENSION 

Composition is an agreement, made upon a sufficient consideration, between a debtor and a creditor, by which the creditor accepts a part of the debt due to him, in satisfaction of the whole.

A composition may be made with one member of a firm which has been dissolved, or with one of several joint debtors, and he be released thereby, without thereby releasing the other members of the firm or joint debtors. Act 1862; 3 Purd. 3462, pl. 13.

EXTENSION AGREEMENTS 

AN EXTENSION AGREEMENT, also called a "letter of license," is an instrument of writing made by creditors to their debtor, by which they bind themselves to allow him longer time than he had a right to for the payment of his debts; and that they will not arrest, or molest him in his person or property, till after the expiration of such additional time. 

Letter of License from Creditors 

KNOW ALL MEN BY THESE PRESENTS, that we, who have hereunto set our hands and seals, creditors of S. R., of -, grocer, taking into consideration that, by reason of losses and misfortunes, he, the said S. R., has not at present wherewith to pay and satisfy us our several debts, do therefore, upon the request of him, the said S. R., severally and respectively, agree and bind ourselves, our heirs, executors and administrators, to accept and take of him, the said S. R., all such debts and sums of money as he doth owe unto us, and every of us, respectively, by four even and equal payments or portions, that is to say: the first payment to be made in one year

next ensuing the date hereof; the second payment in two years next ensuing; the third payment in three years next ensuing; and the last payment or residue of such debts to be made in four years next ensuing the date hereof.

And we do further severally and respectively agree not to arrest, sue, implead, attach or prosecute, by any manner of ways or means whatsoever, the said S. R., or his goods or effects, unless default shall happen to be made in payment of the debts aforesaid on the several days and times above limited, under forfeiture and loss of such of our debts and sums of money for which we shall so arrest, sue, implead, attach or prosecute. 

Witness, &c.

Pennsylvania. The reasons for this condition were (1) the prevalence of the bailment for all purposes which a sale might cover and (2) the fact that the sale invested the vendee with an 22

attachable interest in the property. No protection was afforded the conditional vendor as against either the assignee or the creditor of the vendee. 

On May 12, 1925, however, the legislature passed acts giving conditional sales a legally understandable status. (Act 12 May, 1925, P. L. 603.) (Note: The Act of 1925, P. L. 722, relating to sales of chattels attached or to be attached to realty, was repealed by the Act of 1927, P. L. 979.) It requires the filing in the office of the prothonotary of the contract or a copy thereof in order that it serve as notice to a purchaser or creditor of the vendee. Ten days' grace after the sale is allowed the vendor to file the contract.

Retaking and compulsory resale is allowed by the act after default and 20 to 40 days' notice. If the vendor retakes without notice, he must retain the goods for ten days for redemption by the vendee. Option is also given the vendor to retake subject to no redemption and repay the vendee all payments made. 

The many burdens placed upon the vendor by these acts makes such contracts much less useful than they would ordinarily be expected to be. Full protection can still be had for the vendor by the use of the well established bailment lease (which see). 

The recent case of Stern & Co. v. Paul, 96 Super. Ct. 112, upheld the legality of these instruments despite the acts cited herein.

CONDITIONS OF SALE 

Conditions of sale are the terms upon which the vendor of property by auction proposes to sell it. 

The conditions for the sale of real estate should be in writing, and the purchaser should sign a written acknowledgment of his purchase.

A bidder may withdraw his bid at any time before the property is struck off to him.

If a puffer be employed to bid at an auction, it is a fraud on the real bidders and they are not bound. 

An administrator or other trustee, cannot bid or buy at his own sale without leave of the court. If he wishes to buy he should apply to the court for leave to bid.

Where a buyer at auction fails to complete his purchase, in order to render him liable for loss on resale, the terms of the second sale must not be clogged with terms likely to lower the price.

CONSTABLES 

A CONSTABLE is an executive and ministerial officer of the law within his township, ward, or borough. 

The office is derived from that of the Lord High Constable of England, formerly an officer of great dignity, and vested with

CONSTABLES 

691 high powers to preserve order and enforce the authority of law throughout the kingdom.

The powers and duties of constables relate principally to criminal matters, although, in this country, many duties of a civil nature are by Act of Assembly conferred upon them. Constables are conservators of the peace within their jurisdiction and may apprehend all breakers of the law, and bring them before the proper authorities to answer for their conduct. 

1 Blackstone's Com. 349. It is their duty to keep the public peace in their several districts; and for that purpose they are armed with very large powers of arresting and imprisoning, of breaking open doors, and the like, when such acts are necessary to prevent murder, riots, and violent breaches of the peace. 

1 Penna. Blackstone, 181.

A constable may, without a warrant, apprehend an offender for treason, felony, breach of the peace, and some misdemeanors less than felony, when committed in his view. 1 Hale, 587; 

1 East, P. C. 303; 8 Ser. & Rawle, 47. But he cannot arrest of his own authority after the affray is over. 2 Camp. 367, 371; 

2 Lord Raym. 1296: 1 Chit. Crim. Law. 20 a 24.

He may also, upon the information of others, arrest a supposed offender, without any positive charge, on his own knowledge of the circumstances on which the suspicion is founded; but he does so at his peril, unless he can show that a felony has been committed by some person, as well as the reasonableness of the suspicion that the party arrested is guilty. 1 Chit. Cr. 

L. 27; 6 Binn. R. 316; 2 Hale, 91, 92; 1 East, P. C. 301. He has power, also, to call others to his assistance. If a constable have notice that a burglary has been committed, it is his duty to pursue the felon immediately, though in the night. Cro. Eliz. 652.

At common law, it was the duty of constables to attend the courts of jail delivery and the sessions of the peace for the respective counties, to return warrants and present offenses. 

Cr. Cir. Comp. 34. The duty of attending the county courts is now enforced and regulated, in this country, by statutory provisions.

In Pennsylvania, it is the duty of constables to make returns, on oath or affirmation, to the Court of Quarter Sessions of the proper county, at every term, of all roads in his district which

CONSTABLES 

are out of order, index boards to roads not up, bastard children that have been born, and game killed out of season; of all tippling, disorderly, or gambling houses within said district; of all disturbances of the peace which have occurred at elections; and of all tavern-keepers and retailers of merchandise in said district. The return is to be presented and sworn to in open court. 

A constable is bound to pursue, search for, and arrest offenders, without other compensation than his legal fees, and cannot recover a reward for arresting a person against whom a warrant has been placed in his hands. 10 Pa. 39.

An action against a constable for an escape is not within the limitation of the Act of 1772. That act protects the officer when acting in obedience to his warrant; not against the consequences of wilful misconduct. 8 Pa. 405.

The refusal, without sufficient excuse, to assist a constable in preventing the escape of a person in his custody, is an indictable offense. 6 Black. 277.

The keeper of a prison is bound to receive a person arrested and brought to him by a constable, and charged with a breach of the peace in his presence. 8 S. & R. 47.

A constable's return to an execution must be made in writing. 5 W. & S. 457. A constable, neglecting to make return of his execution to the Justice on or before the return day thereof, is absolutely fixed for the debt and costs. 1 Ash. 160. But if the constable does not return it in consequence of the request of the plaintiff, it is "sufficient cause" for not rendering judgment against him. 1 Ash. 160. The mere omission of a constable to return his execution within twenty days, does not fix him for the amount of the debt, if he have sufficient reason for the delay, 6 W. & S. 534. See McClain v. Smith, 4 Clark 452.

If a judgment be rendered against a constable, by a justice of the peace, for neglect of duty, a transcript thereof may be filed in the court of common pleas, and a fieri facias be issued thereon, without an execution having previously issued from the justice. 

3 W. 278.

A constable who levies upon and sells property exempted from execution, is liable to an action, although the time when the contract (upon which the judgment was founded) was made, was not endorsed upon the execution. 7 Yerg. 88. 

A sheriff [or constable] who has legally levied an execution on property bound by a lien, has a right to discharge the lien,

BOND 

693 in order to get possession; for his writ gives him every implied power which may be necessary to the execution of it. 13 Pa. 215. 

But if he levy on the goods of a stranger, he is not entitled to give in evidence, in mitigation of damages, the payment, out of the proceeds of sale, of a bill for the freight of the goods levied on. Ibid.

In an action against the sureties of a constable, upon his official bond, to recover the amount of a judgment for which the constable has become liable, the judgment previously obtained against the constable himself is conclusive evidence of the liability of sureties. 8 W. 398.

The sureties of a constable are liable for the act of the officer in levying upon the goods of a stranger. 6 W. & S. 513. 

If a warrant appear, on the face of it, to be illegal, the constable is not bound to execute it. 3 Binn. 43. 

The same rules of law which govern sheriffs in the execution of process from the higher courts, govern constables in the execution of a justice's process, except where some statute intervenes. 2 Cow. 421. Under the Act 27 April, 1911, Purd. (1911) 

361, a summons may be served by any constable of the county, provided the costs of service shall not exceed what they would have been had the summons been served by "the next constable most convenient."

CONSTABLES Returns to Executions 

Every execution should, when returned by the constable, be endorsed in such a way that the endorsement may be a proper return to the execution when entered on the docket of the justice. For example, "Money paid into office." "No goods, and defendant not found." "No goods, and defendant by law exempt from arrest." "Levied, and not sold for want of time." "Levied, and not sold for want of indemnity, the goods levied on being claimed by a third person, D. M." "Levied, sold, and money paid into office." Money paid to plaintiff, whose receipt is on the back of the execution." "Bonded and discharged by the prothonotary." Every return made by the constable should be signed with his name as constable and dated. 66

CORONER CORONER 

The CORONER is an officer of equal antiquity with the sheriff, whose principal duty it is to hold an inquisition, with the assistance of a jury, over the body of any person who may have come to a violent death, or who has died in prison. It is his duty also, in case of the death of the sheriff, or when a vacancy happens in that office, to serve all the writs and processes which the sheriff is usually bound to serve; or when just exception can be taken to the sheriff for suspicion of partiality, as that he is a party to or interested in the event of a suit, &c. 1 Black. 

Com. 349; Bac. Abr. h. t.; 6 Vin. Abr. 242; 3 Com. Dig. 242; 

5 Id. 212. The duties of the coroner are of the greatest consequence to society, both for the purpose of bringing to punishment murderers and other offenders against the lives of the citizens, and of protecting innocent persons from accusations. 

See Bouvier's Law Dict., title "Coroners."

Justices of the peace are also empowered by the Act of Assembly of 27th May, 1841, 1 Purd. 764, to hold inquests on dead bodies where there is no lawfully appointed coroner, or when he is absent from the county or unable to attend, or where his office is held more than ten miles distant from the place where the death occurred or the body was found. A justice, in such cases, is empowered by said act to select, summon, and compel the attendance of jurors and witnesses, and to receive like fees and tax like costs as a coroner, and the inquest has the same force and effect in law; but said fees or costs are not allowed or paid said justices or inquest until the proceedings are submitted to the court of quarter sessions of the proper county, and the said court has adjudged that there was reasonable cause for holding said inquest, and approved of the same. 

Unless an inquiry shows some reason for supposing a felonious destruction of life, no inquest should be held. Pfout's Case, 7 

Pa. C. C. 265; Bender's Case, 8 Pa. C. C. 664.

A justice's return of inquest must show, on its face, his jurisdiction. In re Cor. Inquest, 2 Del. 446.

Witnesses at an inquest are entitled neither to fees nor mileage. No fees or expenses are allowed the coroner, except as provided by the fee bill, 1 Pa. C. C. 14; 2 Del. Co. 446.

BOND 

705 In case of murder or manslaughter, fees, together with mileage from the court-house to the place of viewing the body, are to be paid out of the goods and chattels, lands or tenements of the slayer, if he hath any, otherwise by the county.

In executing processes or writs of any kind, a coroner is allowed the same fees as a sheriff. 1 Purd. 765.
