CORPORATIONS 

CORPORATIONS in Pennsylvania are, with very few exceptions, formed under the provisions of the Act of 29 April, 1874, P. L. 

73, and its supplements, by which they are divided into two

FIRST CLASS 

709 classes, viz, first class, generally designated as those not for profit; and second class, those for profit.

Railroad companies, however, are formed under the Act of 4 April, 1868, P. L. 62. By acts passed since 1874, certain specified types of corporations are permitted to be formed. 

The forms covering corporations of the second class have been arranged so as to show to some extent the sequence of events in the life of a corporation.

The corporations defined in the act as being of "the first class" or those not for profit include corporations formed for (1) public worship, (2) benevolent, charitable, educational or missionary undertaking; (3) literary, medical or scientific; (4) agricultural or horticultural; (5) parks, sports, etc.; (6) social clubs; (7) cemeteries; (8) public or private halls; (9) beneficial or protective associations; (10) fire companies; (11) trade, (12) military; (13) streets and public places; (14) holding corporations for the above. 

Application is made to the court of common pleas in the county where the association will function. By Act of 18 April, 1927, P. L. 309, the provisions of the Corporation Act allowing incorporation by the governor of first-class corporations were repealed. By Act of 18 April, 1929, P. L. 539, real estate holdings have been increased to $350,000.

MERGER AND CONSOLIDATION 

Proceedings to merge and consolidate corporations of the first class are precisely the same as proceedings to amend as heretofore outlined. (See Act 17 Apr. 1876, P. L. 37.)

CHANGE OF NAME 

By the Act of 2 May, 1899, P. L. 160, changes of name are treated as amendments or alterations to the charter of a corporation of the first class.

Preferred Stock of which there shall be issued shares of the par value of $100 each, and Common Stock of which there shall be issued shares of the par value of $100 each. 

Resolved, That such Preferred Stock shall be entitled to a cumulative dividend of per centum per annum; but after such cumulative dividend, with all arrears shall have been paid, it shall not be entitled to any further dividends in any year until dividends aggregating per centum in such year shall have been declared and set aside out of the profits for the Common Stock; that thereafter any additional dividends for such year shall be declared pro rata for the Preferred and Common Stock until the total dividends for such year on both Preferred and Common Stock shall aggregate per centum; that the Preferred Stock shall not

be entitled to dividends in excess of per centum in any year, except when in payment of the arrears of cumulative dividends above provided for; that upon any dissolution or liquidation of the Company or in the event of its insolvency or upon any distribution of capital, there shall be paid to the holders of Preferred Stock the par value thereof, and the amount of all unpaid accrued dividends thereon before any sum shall be paid or any assets distributed among the holders of the Common Stock; and that after the payment to the holders of the 

Preferred Stock of its par value and the unpaid accrued dividends thereon, the remaining assets and funds of the Company shall be divided among and paid to the holders of the Common Stock, according to their respective shares.

BY-LAWS 

743 

BY-LAWS ARTICLE I 

Stockholders 

SECTION 1. Certificates of stock shall be issued to the stockholders and transfers made when required, said certificates to be signed by the President or Vice-President and the Treasurer, registered by the Secretary, and authenticated by the seal of the Company. 

SEC. 2. The stock of the Company shall be transferred only on the books of the Company by the stockholders himself in person, or by his attorney in fact, duly constituted, according to such forms as the Directors may prescribe. The certificates surrendered shall be canceled at time of transfer, and filed with the Treasurer of the Company.

SEC. 3. No transfers of stock shall be made upon the books of the Company for days preceding the date appointed for the payment of any dividend or for any election. Only those persons who appear on the books of the Company as stockholders shall be entitled to receive any dividends or to vote at any meeting or election of the Company*

SEC. 4. Any person or persons desiring a certificate of stock to be issued in lieu of one lost or destroyed, shall, after applying for the same, advertise such loss or destruction in one or more newspapers published in 

Pennsylvania, twice a week for four weeks, stating the number and date of the certificate lost or destroyed, the number of shares represented thereby, and that application has been made to the Board of Directors for a certificate in lieu thereof. The applicant shall then furnish the Board of Directors with an affidavit describing the certificate, its loss or destruction, and advertisement made in conformity therewith, accompanied by a copy of the advertisement, and also a bond of indemnity, with satisfactory personal security, in at least double the *See the Act of 30 April, 1929, P. L. 903.

CORPORATIONS 

amount of the certificate, against any damage that may arise from issuing a new certificate; whereupon the 

Board may direct (one month after the date of appearance of the last advertisement) the issue of a new certificate, of the same tenor with the one alleged to be lost or destroyed, therein specifying that it is in lieu thereof. 

And the application for a new certificate, and the evidence of compliance by the applicant with all the requirements of this by-law, shall be made in such form as shall be satisfactory to the Board of Directors. 

SEC. 5. Each stockholder, at the time of the issuance to him of a stock certificate, shall notify the Secretary in writing of the address to which he wishes notices relating to the business of the Company to be mailed to him. He shall thereafter notify the Secretary of any change in such address.

SEC. 6. The general office of the Company, and also the offices of the President, of the Secretary and of the Treasurer, with the books and papers thereto belonging, shall be at -, Pennsylvania.

ARTICLE II Meetings of Stockholders SECTION 1. The annual meeting of the stockholders shall be held at the general office of the Company, or at such other place in Pennsylvania as the Board of Directors may provide, on the in each year, unless that day be duly designated a legal holiday, in which event the annual meeting shall be held on the following day not a legal holiday. day of

SEC. 2. At the annual meeting of the stockholders there shall be held an election for Directors to serve for the ensuing year, or until their successors be chosen, which election shall be conducted by the judges appointed by the Board of Directors and duly qualified as required by law.

BY-LAWS 

745 

SEC. 3. Special meetings of the stockholders may be called at any time upon the written request of a majority of the Board of Directors; or any stockholder or stockholders holding at least one-tenth in amount of the capital stock of the Company, may at any time apply to the President, or, in his absence, to the Secretary, to call a special meeting of the stockholders; and upon such application, which shall state the object of the meeting, it shall be the duty of the President, or in his absence, the Secretary, to call such meeting within thirty days from date of receipt of the application. 

SEC. 4. At least days' notice shall be given of the time when and place where the annual or any special meeting of the stockholders is to be held. Such notice shall be signed by the Secretary of the Company and mailed to each stockholder at the address last given by him, as herein provided. If no such address be given, notice deposited in the post office, addressed to him at the city in which the general office of the Company is located, shall be sufficient. 

SEC. 5. The notice of every special meeting shall state briefly the special business to come before the meeting, and only such business shall be considered at such meeting, unless with the consent of stockholders holding threefourths of the entire capital stock of the Company. 

SEC. 6. A roll of the stockholders in alphabetical order, together with the last address given and the number of shares held by each stockholder, shall be kept by the Secretary and laid before the stockholders at each of their meetings. Such list shall always be open to the examination of any stockholder at the office of the Company.

SEC. 7. At all stockholders' meetings stockholders may attend and vote either in person or by proxy. All proxies shall be in writing. Partnerships may sign in the name of the partnership, and the signature of the firm by any member thereof shall be valid. No proxy shall be valid. for more than sixty days from the date thereof.

CORPORATIONS 

SEC. 8. The holders for the time being of a majority of the outstanding shares of stock of the Company, appearing either in person or by proxy, shall constitute a quorum for the transaction of business at any annual or special meeting of the stockholders; but the holders of a less number, appearing at the time and place for which such meeting was called may adjourn from time to time for a period not exceeding twenty days. 

SEC. 9. All elections shall be by ballot, unless by unanimous consent the vote be taken viva voce. When by ballot, the record of the name of, and amount of stock represented by, each party voting shall be made and certified to by judges, duly appointed, and shall be kept on file with the archives of the Company, and in case of an election for any officer of the Company elected by the stockholders, a report of the result thereof shall be in like manner made, certified to, and filed. 

SEC. 10. Each Director shall be a stockholder in the 

Company, and shall hold his office, unless removed or disqualified from some cause, until the next stated annual meeting, and thereafter until his successor shall be chosen.

SEC. 11. The stockholders of the Company may, by a vote of three-fourths of all the stock, at any meeting duly convened and called for the purpose, remove any one or more of the Directors or other officers of the Company, and may then proceed to fill the vacancy or vacancies caused by such removal or removals. 

ARTICLE III 

Directors

SECTION 1. The number of the Directors of the Com pany shall be 

The Secretary and Treasurer of the Company shall be ex officio Secretary and Treasurer of the Board of Directors. 

SEC. 2. The first regular meeting of the Board of Di rectors shall be held each year immediately upon the ad-

BY-LAWS 

747 journment of the meeting of the stockholders in that year at which the Directors are elected. Regular meetings of the Board of Directors shall also be held at the general office of the Company, on the day of each month, unless otherwise designated by the Board. Meetings may be called at any other time by the President, and shall be called by him, or, in his absence, by the Secretary, on the written request of three members of the Board, to be convened at such time and place as may be appointed. 

A majority of the Board shall constitute a business quorum.

SEC. 3. At the first regular meeting of the Board of 

Directors after their election, they shall elect a President, Vice-President, Secretary and Treasurer of the Company to serve for the ensuing year and thereafter until their successors shall be chosen. The President shall be and each other officer may be, a Director of the Company. Any two of said offices may be held by the same person.

SEC. 4. The President shall preside at all meetings of the Board of Directors, preserve order and regulate debates according to parliamentary rules, and appoint all committees not otherwise ordered by the Board. In the absence of the President, the Vice-President shall preside. In the absence of both President and Vice-President, a President pro tempore may be appointed by the Board.

SEC. 5. The order of business shall be as follows: 

When a quorum appears, the President shall call the 

Board to order.

The minutes shall be read, and considered as approved if there is no motion to amend them. 

Reports of Committees. 

Reports of officers of the Company.

Miscellaneous communications. 

Unfinished business. 

New business.

CORPORATIONS SEC. 6. The Board of Directors shall have power, for sufficient cause, to remove from an office or position, other than that of Director, any officer, agent or employee of the Company by a vote of a majority of the entire Board, and shall have power to fill the vacancies so occurring or created, and for the purpose of filling any vacancy, a vote of the majority of the whole Board shall be sufficient.

SEC. 7. The Board of Directors may, by a vote of a majority of the Board, accept the resignation of any one or more of its members, or of any officer or officers of the Company, and have power forthwith to fill the vacancy or vacancies, so created, by the election of a successor or successors to such resigning member or members, or officer or officers of the Company. But if the officer so resigning be an officer elected by the stockholders, a special meeting of the stockholders shall be forthwith called, to convene within thirty days, to hold an election. to fill the vacancy.

SEC. 8. The Board of Directors shall fix the compensa tion of the officers and agents of the Company and the wages of other employees.

SEC. 9. The Board of Directors may appoint from their own number an Executive Committee, who shall serve during the pleasure of the Board, and to whom may be intrusted by the Board such business as may be lawfully delegated to such a committee. The Executive Committee shall report promptly to the Board all actions taken by it. Vacancies therein shall be filled by the Board. 

ARTICLE IV Officers SECTION 1. The President shall be a stockholder and 

Director of the Company and shall hold a vigilant superintendence over all the affairs of the Company, and shall have general supervision and control of all the employees of the Company, and shall prescribe their duties when not otherwise provided for.

BY-LAWS 

749 He shall have custody of the seal of the Company, and attend generally to its executive business, under the direction of the Board, and be ex officio a member of all committees.

All letters, reports or other papers relating to the business of the Company, received by the Secretary or by the Treasurer, shall be submitted to the President, and when practicable, all instructions emanating from either of those officers shall be first approved by the President or by the Board of Directors. 

SEC. 2. The Vice-President shall be a stockholder of the Company, and shall, in the absence or disability of the President perform his duties. He shall also perform any of the duties imposed by these by-laws on the President which the President may delegate or the Board of Directors may assign to him. 

SEC. 3. The Secretary shall be present at all meetings of the stockholders and the Board, take minutes of the proceedings, and record the same in a suitable book for preservation. He shall notify the members of all regular and called meetings of the Board, and furnish the chairman of each committee with a copy of the resolution appointing such committee, and shall perform all duties which are imposed on him by these by-laws or are customary and incident to the office of Secretary in like corporations.

He shall have charge of the books, maps, letters, deeds, &c., in the office of the Company. 

SEC. 4. The Treasurer shall give bonds, with one or more satisfactory sureties, in such sum as the Board may from time to time require, for the faithful performance of all his duties. The cost of procuring such bonds shall be defrayed by the Company. 

He shall keep a regular set of books, containing the accounts of the Company, and of all the funds that may pass through his hands.

He shall make reports of his receipts and disbursements at each regular meeting of the Board of Directors,

CORPORATIONS 

in such form and detail as the Board may direct; shall present a complete statement of his accounts for the previous fiscal year, at the meeting of the Board immediately preceding the annual meeting of the stockholders; and shall attend to such other duties as the President or the Board of Directors may from time to time require. 

His books shall at all times be open to the inspection of the President, the Vice-President or any member of the 

Board. 

The money of the Company shall be deposited by the Treasurer in such bank or banks or other depository as the Directors of the Company may from time to time prescribe. No money deposited in any bank or other depository to the Company's credit shall be withdrawn, except upon a check executed in such a way as the Board of Directors may from time to time prescribe, or by vouchers duly signed in such form as may be approved by the Board of Directors. 

SEC. 5. No officer, agent or employee of the Company shall have power to make, indorse or accept any draft, promissory note, bill of exchange or other instrument for the payment of money in the name or on behalf of the Company, except for the purposes of its usual business or when specially authorized by a majority of the Board of Directors. All such instruments shall be signed on behalf of the Company in the manner provided in these by-laws in the case of checks. But any such instrument may be indorsed in the name of the Company for deposit in bank or for collection on its behalf by any officer of the Company.

SEC. 6. In addition to the officers elected by the stockholders and the Board of Directors, there may be appointed by the President such other officers and agents as may, in his judgment, be deemed necessary for the effective transaction of the business of the Company, subject to the approval of the Board at the next meeting subsequent to such appointment.

ARTICLE V. 

Corporate Seal 

The common or corporate seal of the Company is, and until otherwise ordered by the Board of Directors, shall be, an impression upon paper or wax, bearing the words 

ARTICLE VI Amendments 

These by-laws may be amended at any regular or special meeting of the stockholders; but no alteration or amendment shall be made in them unless notice in writing, stating the terms of the proposed amendment, has been given to the Secretary at least thirty days before the date of such meeting, and notice has been sent, at least fifteen days before such meeting, to each stockholder at the address last given by him to the Secretary, setting out in full the existing by-law and the proposed amendment thereto. It shall be the duty of the Secretary to send such notice to the stockholders; but such notice may be sent by the stockholder proposing the amendment.

Concerning the Trustee 

SECTION 1. The Trustee shall not be answerable for the default or misconduct of any agent or attorney ap-

TRUST DEED 

779 pointed by or in pursuance hereof, if such agent or attorney shall have been selected with reasonable care; nor for any act done by the Company with respect to the property hereby pledged by virtue of any power reserved to it by the provisions hereof; nor for anything whatever in connection with this trust, except for willful misconduct or gross negligence. The Trustee shall not be under any obligation to take any action towards the execution or enforcement of the trusts hereby created, which, in its opinion, shall be likely to involve it in any expense or liability, unless one or more holders of the debentures hereby secured shall, as often as required by the Trustee, furnish it reasonable indemnity against such expense or liability; nor shall the Trustee be required to take notice of any default hereunder unless notified in writing of such default by the holders of at least twenty-five per centum in amount of the debentures hereby secured and then outstanding, or to take any action in respect of any default unless requested to take action in respect thereof by a writing signed by the holders of not less than twentyfive per centum in amount of the debentures hereby secured and then outstanding, and tendered reasonable indemnity as aforesaid, anything herein contained to the contrary notwithstanding; but the foregoing provisions of this Section are intended only for the protection of the Trustee and shall not be construed to limit or affect any discretion or power by any provision of this Indenture given to the Trustee to determine whether or not it shall take action in respect of any default or any power or discretion of the Trustee to take action in respect of any default without such notice or request from debenture holders. The Trustee shall not be responsible for the recording of this Indenture and shall not be required to file the same as a chattel mortgage. 

The Trustee shall be entitled to reasonable compensation for all services rendered by it in the execution of the trusts hereby created and the Company agrees to pay

CORPORATIONS 

such compensation, as well as all expenses necessarily incurred or disbursed by the Trustee hereunder. 

SECTION 2. The Trustee or any Trustee hereafter ap pointed may resign and be discharged of the trusts created by this Indenture by giving notice thereof to the Company and to the debenture holders, by publication at least twice a week for four successive weeks in one newspaper, at that time published in Pennsylvania, and by due execution of the conveyance herein required. 

The Trustee may be removed at any time by an instrument in writing under the hands of holders of seventy-five per centum in amount of the debentures hereby secured and then outstanding. 

SECTION 3. In case at any time the Trustee or any 

Trustee hereafter appointed, shall resign or shall be removed, or otherwise shall become incapable of acting, a successor or successors may be appointed by the holders of a majority in amount of the debentures hereby secured and then outstanding, by an instrument or concurrent instruments signed by such debenture holders or their attorneys in fact duly authorized; provided, nevertheless, and it is hereby agreed and declared that in case at any time there shall be a vacancy in the office of Trustee hereunder, the Company, by an instrument executed by order of its Board of Directors, may appoint a Trustee to fill such vacancy until a new Trustee shall be appointed by the debenture holders as herein authorized. Thereupon the Company shall publish notice of such appointment once a week for six consecutive weeks in a newspaper published in Pennsylvania, and any Trustee so appointed by the Company shall immediately and without further act be superseded by a Trustee appointed in the manner above provided by the holders of a majority in amount of the debentures hereby secured and then outstanding prior to the expiration of one year after such publication of notice. 

Any such new Trustee appointed hereunder shall

TRUST DEED 

781 execute, acknowledge and deliver to the Trustee last in office, and also to the Company, an instrument accepting such appointment hereunder, and thereupon such new Trustee without any further act, deed or conveyance, shall become vested with all the estates, properties, rights, powers, trusts, duties and obligations of its predecessor in the trust hereunder with like effect as if originally named as Trustee herein; but nevertheless on the written request of the new Trustee, the Trustee ceasing to act shall execute, and deliver an instrument transferring to such new Trustee, upon the trusts herein expressed, all the estates, properties, rights, powers and trusts of the Trustee so resigning, or removed, and shall duly assign, transfer and deliver any property, contracts and moneys held by such Trustee to the new Trustee so appointed in its place; and upon request of any such new 

Trustee shall make, execute, acknowledge and deliver any and all instruments in writing for more fully and certainly vesting in and confirming to such new Trustee all such estates, properties, rights, powers and duties. 

ARTICLE VIII Termination of Trust SECTION 1. If (1) when the debentures hereby secured, shall have become due and payable, the Company shall well and truly pay or cause to be paid the whole amount of the principal moneys and interest due upon all the debentures and coupons for interest thereon hereby secured and then outstanding, or shall provide for such payment by depositing with the Trustee hereunder for the payment of such debentures and coupons, the entire amount due thereon for principal and interest; or if (2) the Company shall at any earlier date, have redeemed and retired in the manner hereinbefore provided, all of such debentures with interest due up to the time of such redemption; and if in either case the Company shall also pay or cause

CORPORATIONS 

to be paid all other sums payable hereunder by it, and shall well and truly keep and perform all the things herein required to be kept and performed by it according to the true intent and meaning of this Indenture, then and in that case all property, rights and interests hereby assigned, conveyed, and pledged shall revert to the Company and the estate, rights, title and interest of the Trustee shall thereupon cease, determine and become void and the Trustee in such case on demand of the Company, and at its cost and expense, shall enter satisfaction of this Indenture upon the record; otherwise the same shall be, continue and remain in full force and virtue. 

ARTICLE IX Miscellaneous Provisions SECTION 1. All the covenants, stipulations, promises and agreements, in this Indenture contained, by or in behalf of the Company shall bind such Company, its successors and assigns, whether so expressed or not. 

SECTION 2. For every purpose of this Indenture, including the execution, issue and use of any and all debentures hereby secured, the term "Company" includes and means not only the party of the first part hereto, but also any successor corporation. Every such successor corporation shall possess, and from time to time may exercise, each and every right, and power hereunder of the Company in its name or otherwise. 

SECTION 3. Except when otherwise indicated, the words 

"the Trustee" or "said Trustee' or other equivalent term as used in this Indenture, shall be held and construed to mean the Trustee or Trustee for the time being, whether original or successor, and the words "Trustee," "debenture," "debenture holder" and "holder" shall include the plural as well as the singular number, and the term "majority" shall signify "majority in amount,' whether or not so expressed.

D., 1909, which Acts are hereby incorporated into and made a part of this agreement. 

Fourteenth. The said consolidated or new corporation shall be subject to and regulated by the corporate rights, privileges, franchises, duties and obligations existing under and by virtue of each and any and all of the several certificates of incorporation and Letters Patent thereunder issued to each of the said corporations, parties hereto, and the Acts of Assembly of the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, relating to each of the said corporations parties hereto. 

Fifteenth. It shall be the duty of the Directors of the new or consolidated corporation forthwith to adopt By- Laws for said corporation, and from time to time to alter, amend and add to the same. Such Directors shall also determine the form of the official seal and of the certificates of stock of such corporation. 

Sixteenth. The and appoint Company doth hereby constitute to be its attorney, for it and in its name and as for its corporate act and deed, to acknowledge this agreement before any person having authority 26

CORPORATIONS 

by the laws of the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania to take such acknowledgments, to the intent that the same may be duly recorded. 

Seventeenth. The stitute and appoint Company doth hereby conto be its attorney, for it and in its name and as and for its corporate act and deed, to acknowledge this agreement before any person having authority by the laws of the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania to take such acknowledgments, to the intent that the same may be duly recorded. 

Eighteenth. Upon the consummation of this act of consolidation in the manner provided by law, all and singular the rights, privileges and franchises of each of the said corporations, parties hereto, and all the property, real, personal and mixed, and all accounts and bills receivable and all other rights and choses in action belonging to each of the said corporations, parties hereto, shall be taken, deemed and considered to be sold, transferred, assigned and conveyed to and vested in the said consolidated or new corporation without further act or deed, to the intent that the said consolidated or new corporation shall become the owner of and have vested in it all the said rights, privileges, franchises, properties, choses and rights in action now belonging to and owned by the said corporations, parties hereto, or to which said corporations are or may be entitled. PROVIDED HOWEVER, that all the rights of creditors and all liens upon the property of each of the said corporations, parties hereto, shall continue unimpaired and the respective constituent corporations, parties hereto, shall be deemed to be in existence to preserve the same, and all debts, duties and liabilities of each of the said constituent corporations, parties hereto, shall henceforth attach to the said new corporation and may be enforced against it to the same extent and by the same process as if said debts, duties and liabilities had been contracted by the said consolidated or new corporation.

(Corporate Seal.) SALES OF REAL ESTATE 

The power to acquire and sell real estate of a manufacturing corporation has been vested in the board of directors by the Act of June 12, 1919, P. L. 442. The

CORPORATIONS 

consent of the stockholders need not be had where the corporation sells for a valuable consideration to a resident of the Commonwealth. 

PROXIES 

By Act of March 5, 1903, P. L. 14, all stockholders may vote by proxy duly executed and witnessed, provided the said proxy be not more than two months old at the time of voting. And this right cannot be abridged by by-law or amendment.

(Date.) COVENANTS AND RESTRICTIONS 

A COVENANT is an agreement between two or more persons, entered into in writing and under seal, whereby either party stipulates for the truth of certain facts, or promises to perform or give something to the other, or to abstain from the performance of certain things. 

In a promise or contract not under seal, a consideration must be shown; in a covenant under seal, no consideration is necessary to give it validity, even in a court of equity. 

The general requisites to a covenant are, 1st, proper parties; 

2dly, an agreement; 3dly, a legal promise; and 4thly, that it be properly executed. 

1st. The parties must be such as by law can enter into a contract. If, either for want of understanding [as in the case of an idiot or lunatic; or in the case of an infant (under 21 years of age) where the contract is not for his benefit]; or where there is understanding, but, owing to certain causes [as coverture, in the case of a married woman (except where Acts of Assembly have conferred power upon the wife), or duress, in every case], the parties are not competent, they cannot bind themselves. 

2dly. There must be an agreement. The assent or consent must be mutual; for the agreement would be incomplete if either party withheld his assent to any of its terms. The assent to the

HEAD NOTE 

845 contract necessarily supposes a free, fair, serious exercise of the reasoning faculty. Now, if from any cause, this free assent be not given, the contract is void. 

3dly. A covenant against any positive law, or public policy, is generally void. As an example of the first is a covenant by one man that he will rob another; and of the last, a covenant by a merchant or tradesman that he will not follow his occupation or calling. This, if it be unlimited, is absolutely void; but if the covenant be that he shall not pursue his business in a particular place, as that he will not trade in the City of Philadelphia, the covenant is no longer against public policy. A covenant to do an impossible thing is also void. In 4thly. To make a covenant, it must, according to the definition above given, be by deed, or under seal. The law does not seem to have appropriated any set of words as absolutely required in creating a covenant. Any words which manifest the intention of the parties to perform an act are sufficient. 

Pennsylvania it is declared by statute that the words "grant, bargain, and sell," shall amount to a covenant that the grantor was seized of an estate in fee, free from all encumbrances done or suffered by him, and for quiet enjoyment against his acts. 

But it has been adjudged that those words in the Pennsylvania statute of 1715 did not amount to a general warranty, but merely to a covenant that the grantor had not done any act, nor created any encumbrance whereby the estate might be defeated. 

Section 3 of the Act of 1 April, 1909, P. L. 91, 5 Purd. 5394, provides that, in any deed thereafter executed, the words "grant and convey,' or either of said words, "shall be adjudged an express covenant to the grantee, his heirs and assigns; to wit, That the grantor was seized of an indefeasible estate in fee simple in the property conveyed, freed from incumbrances done or suffered from the grantor, as also for quiet enjoyment against the grantor, his heirs and assigns, unless limited by express words contained in said deed." Section 4 provides that a covenant by the grantor that he "will warrant generally the property hereby conveyed" shall have the same effect as a covenant of general warranty written out in full. And Section 5 provides that the words "will warrant specially the property hereby conveyed" shall have the same effect as a covenant of special warranty. 

---

Covenants are express or implied. 1st An express covenant, or a covenant in fact, is one expressly agreed between the parties and inserted in the deed. The law does not require any particular form to create an express covenant. The formal word "covenant" is therefore not indispensably requisite. The words, "I oblige,' agree," or, "I bind myself to pay so much such a day, and so much such another day," are held to be covenants; and so are the words of a bond. But words importing merely an order or direction that other persons should pay a sum of money are not a covenant. "" (( A covenant in law, is one which the law intends and implies, though it be not expressed in words. There are some words which of themselves do not import an express covenant, yet, being made use of in certain contracts, have a similar operation, and are called covenants in law. They are as effectually binding on the parties as if expressed in the most unequivocal terms. A few examples will fully explain this. If a lessor demise and grant to his lessee a house or lands for a certain term, the law will imply a covenant on the part of the lessor that the lessee shall during the term quietly enjoy the same against all encumbrances. And the words "yielding and paying" in a lease imply a covenant, on the part of a lessee, that he will pay the rent. 

1. General Form of a Covenant by One Person 

And the said John Jones, for himself, his heirs, executors, and administrators, [or as the case may require], doth hereby covenant to and with the said William Burns, his heirs, executors, administrators, and assigns, [or as the case may require], by these presents, as follows; that, &c. [here insert whatever is agreed upon]. 

2. General Form of a Covenant by Two or More Persons 

Jointly and Severally And the said John Jones and John Doe, for themselves, their heirs, executors, and administrators, [or as the case may require], do hereby jointly and severally covenant to and with the said William Burns, his heirs, executors, administrators, and assigns, [or as the case may

PARTIES 

847 require], by these presents, as follows [here insert whatever is agreed upon]. 

3. Covenant by a Husband for Himself and Wife 

And the said John Jones, for himself, his heirs, executors, and administrators, and for and on behalf of the said Mary Jones, and her heirs, executors, and administrators, doth covenant with the said William Burns, his heirs, executors, administrators, and assigns, as follows; that, &c. [here insert agreement]. 

4. Covenant by Several Individuals Where Each Party 

Confines His Covenant to His Own Portion of an Estate And the said John Jones, for himself, his heirs, executors, and administrators, for the estate, right, title, quiet enjoyment, and further assurance of one-sixth part of the said hereditaments and premises; and the said John 

Doe, for himself, his heirs, executors, and administrators, for the estate, right, title, quiet, enjoyment, and further assurance of one-sixth part of the said hereditaments and premises; and the said [here continue to state the remainder of the parties in the same way as the first two above] do, and each and every of them doth, severally, but not jointly, covenant, each for himself and his heirs, with the said William Burns, his heirs, executors, administrators, and assigns that, [here state what is covenanted]. 

5. Another Form of Covenant by Several Individuals 

Severally but Not Jointly 

And the said John Jones, John Doe, Richard Roe, and

John Flagg, for themselves severally and respectively, and for their several and respective heirs, executors, and administrators; but not jointly, or the one for the other, or others of them, do covenant, each for himself and his heirs, with the said William Burns, his heirs, executors, administrators, and assigns, by these presents in manner following, [here insert fully the covenants].

6. Covenant Asserting Title to Real Estate, by a Tenant for Life and a Tenant in Fee of the Reversion, Who 

Join in a Deed.

And the said John Jones and William Jones, for themselves respectively, and for their respective heirs, executors, and administrators, but not jointly, or one for the other, do hereby covenant each for himself and his heirs, with the said William Burns, his heirs, executors, administrators, and assigns, that at the execution of these presents, they, the said John Jones and William Jones are lawfully seized of the granted premises in manner following, that is to say, the said John Jones is seized thereof as tenant by the curtesy, and the said William Jones is seized in fee simple of reversion expectant upon the determination of the said estate by the curtesy, &c. 

7. Covenant Asserting Title to Real Estate, by Two 

Vendors Severally, but Not Jointly And the said John Jones and William Jones, for themselves respectively, and not jointly, or one for the other, do hereby covenant each for himself and his heirs with the said William Burns, that they, the said John Jones and William Jones, at the delivery hereof, are and stand, and each of them is and standeth lawfully seized of and in the several parts and proportions of and in the said messuage, tenement, or tract of land herein described, &c. 

8. Covenant to Stand Seized of Premises Not Well 

Conveyed, for the Uses in the Deed Mentioned And the said John Jones doth, for himself and his heirs, covenant and agree, for the consideration aforesaid, to and with the said William Burns and his heirs, that the said John Jones and his heirs shall and will, from and after the 

 day of 9 stand and be seized to the several uses in and by these premises limited and declared, according to the true meaning hereof, of and in such part

ESTATES 

849 and so much of the premises as for any cause or defect whatsoever shall not be well and sufficiently conveyed and assured unto the said William Burns and his heirs, to the uses as aforesaid, before the day of aforesaid, and to no other use, intent, or purpose. 

9. Covenant by Trustees, Where They Join in a Conveyance, that They Have Done No Act to Encumber 

And the said John Jones, John Doe, and John Flagg, the parties hereto of the first part, [or as the case may be], separately and apart, each for himself, his heirs, executors, and administrators, and not jointly, nor the one for the other, or others for them, but each of them for his own acts only, do covenant with the said William Burns, his heirs and assigns, that they, the said John 

Jones, John Doe, and John Flagg have not, nor hath either of them, at any time heretofore, done or suffered any act, matter, or thing whatsoever, whereby the said premises hereby granted and released, or any part thereof, is, or can be, impeached or encumbered in title, estate, or otherwise howsoever. 

10. Covenant for Quiet Enjoyment

And the said John Jones, party hereto, for himself, his heirs, executors, and administrators, doth covenant to and with the said William Burns, his heirs and assigns, by these presents, that he, the said William Burns, his heirs and assigns, shall and may, from time to time, and at all times forever hereafter, peaceably and quietly have, hold, and enjoy all and singular the said premises hereby granted and released, without the hindrance, denial, or interruption of any person or persons lawfully claiming, or to claim any right, title, or interest at law or in equity, in, to, or out of the same, or any part thereof. 

11. Covenant for Further Assuring Conveyance of Real Estate

And the said John Jones, for himself, his heirs, executors, and administrators, doth hereby further covenant

with the said William Burns, his heirs and assigns, that the said John Jones, his heirs, executors, administrators, and assigns, at the request and at the charges of the said William Burns, his heirs or assigns, shall and will from time to time, and at all times hereafter, execute, acknowledge and deliver, or cause to be executed, acknowledged, and delivered all and every such further and other acts, conveyances, and assurances in law, for the better assuring to the said William Burns, his heirs and assigns, of the premises, in manner as above conveyed, or mentioned and intended to be conveyed, as the said William Burns, his heirs and assigns, or his or their counsel learned in the law, shall reasonably advise and require. 

12. Covenant of Warranty 

And the said John Jones, for himself, his heirs, executors, and administrators, doth hereby covenant, promise, grant, and agree, to and with the said William Burns, his heirs and assigns, by these presents, that he, the said John Jones and his heirs, the said above mentioned and described messuage and tract of land, hereditaments, and appurtenances, hereby granted or mentioned, or intended so to be, unto the said William Burns, his heirs and assigns, against him, the said John Jones, and his heirs, and against all and every other person and persons whomsoever, lawfully claiming or to claim the same or any part thereof, [*by, from, or under him, them, or any of them], shall and will warrant and for ever defend by these presents. 

13. Covenant Against Encumbrances 

And the said John Jones, for himself, his heirs, executors, and administrators, doth covenant, promise, grant, *This, without the words in brackets, is a general warranty that is to say, a warranty against all the world; but with the words in brackets, it is a special warranty, that is to say, a warranty against the grantor and his heirs only.

16. Covenant Restricting the Type of Building, &c. 

It is expressly covenanted and agreed by and between the parties hereto that no building other than one dwelling house to cost not less than $ shall ever be erected upon the within described premises nor shall such building approach the front building line nearer than feet, nor the side lines of said lot nearer than feet, except that bay windows or steps may extend for a distance of feet from the lines as hereby established. 

17. Covenant to Build 

The said grantee (or lessee), for himself, his heirs, executors, administrators and assigns, doth covenant, promise, and agree, to and with the said grantor, (or lessor), his heirs and assigns by these presents, that he, the said grantee (or lessee), his heirs or assigns, shall and will, within months from the date hereof, erect and build on the said hereby granted (or demised) lot a dwelling house of the value of dollars to secure the yearly rent thereby reserved (or as the case may be). 

18. Covenant that Lessee May Deduct Out of His Rent the Amount Paid by Him for Taxes and Repairs 

And also that it shall and may be lawful, to and for the said William Burns, his executors, administrators, and

853 assigns, to retain, deduct, and keep out of every year's rent, agreed to be paid to the said John Jones, his heirs or assigns, as aforesaid, so much money as he, the said William Burns, his executors, administrators, or assigns, shall from time to time, during the said term, have paid for taxes on said premises, or such repairs, amendments, and additions by him made or done, or cause to be made or done, in and about said premises, by and with the consent or direction of the said John Jones, his heirs or assigns; or for repairs to said premises without the direction or consent of the said John Jones, his heirs or assigns, provided said repairs are necessary to keep the said premises in proper tenantable condition. 

19. Covenant that Lessee Shall Pay Taxes

That he, the said William Burns, his executors, administrators, and assigns, shall and will from time to time, and at all times, during the said term hereby granted, well and truly pay, in addition to the sum hereinbefore named for rent, all rates, taxes, in excess of those for the current year, [or as the case may be], duties, charges, and assessments whatsoever, that shall or may be assessed, charged, rated, or imposed on the said hereby demised premises, or any part thereof, and thereof and therefrom save harmless and keep indemnified the said John Jones, his executors, administrators, and assigns; and also his and their lands and tenements. 

20. Covenant that Lessor Shall Insure the Premises against Fire and Rebuild in Case of Destruction or 

Damage by Fire. 

And that he, the said John Jones, his executors, administrators, and assigns, shall and will, at his and their own proper costs and charges, from time to time sufficiently insure all and every the messuages or tenements, erections or buildings which shall be erected and built upon the said piece or parcel of ground hereby demised, or any part thereof, from casualties by fire, during the

then remainder of the said term hereby granted, in some one or more of the public offices kept for that purpose in Philadelphia; and in case the said messuages or tenements, erections or buildings, or any of them, or any part of them, shall at any time or times during the said term be burnt down, destroyed, or damaged by fire, shall and will immediately afterwards rebuild, or well and sufficiently repair the same." 

21. Covenant that Lessee Shall Not Be Chargeable for 

Any Accident by Fire

It is covenanted, concluded, and agreed, by and between the said parties to these presents, that the said lessee, his executors, administrators, or assigns, shall not by virtue of these presents, or any article, clause or agreement herein contained, be chargeable or charged with, or answerable for any accidents of fire which shall happen during the continuance of this demise, and that such accidents of fire are wholly excepted out of the before mentioned covenants for keeping and leaving the premises in repair; and the said lessee, his executors, administrators, and assigns are not by color of any clause in these presents contained, to answer or make good any such accidents or any damage occasioned thereby, but that the same are to be borne by the said lessor, his heirs or assigns; anything in these presents contained to the contrary in any wise notwithstanding.

24. Covenant that Lessee Shall Use the Hay, &c., on the

Premises, and Spread the Dung thereon And also that he, the said William Burns, shall and will, during the continuance of this lease, use on the said demised premises all the hay and straw arising therefrom, and shall spread and bestow all the compost and dung which shall be made thereby upon the said premises in a proper manner, save only the compost or dung to be made in the last year of this lease, which the said William Burns shall leave upon the said premises, unto and for the said John Jones, without being paid or allowed anything for the same.

Premises within the Term.

And lastly, it is hereby covenanted and agreed, by and between the said parties hereto, and it is the true intent and meaning of these presents, that if the said William Burns, his executors, administrators, or assigns, shall be minded and desirous to leave, yield, and give up the said premises hereby demised, at the end of years or years next after the commencement of this present demise or lease, and shall give months' notice or thereof, under his or their hands, unto the said John Jones, his heirs or assigns, immediately preceding either of the said terms of years, this present indenture and the term and estate hereby granted shall cease, determine, and be utterly void; anything herein contained to the contrary notwithstanding.

PRELIMINARY NOTE 

On October 4, 1915, pursuant to authority granted him by the Act of April 23, 1915, P. L. 177, the Governor appointed three 

Commissioners "to codify and revise the law of decedents' estates."

The suggestions contained in their report, submitted on February 1, 1917, have been incorporated in the following acts of June 7, 1917: 

Intestate Act, P. L. 429.

Partition Act, P. L. 337. 

Fiduciaries Act, P. L. 447. 

Revised Price Act, P. L. 388.

Wills Act, P. L. 403. 

Register of Wills Act, P. L. 415. 

Orphans' Court Act, P. L. 363. 

It. necessarily follows that the practice and forms used in practice have been changed considerably. The editors have herein revised all the forms in the last edition and brought them to date so as to eliminate the necessity of reference to any other book of forms on the particular subject. Citations to the acts have been appended to the forms where deemed necessary.

S., G. S. and F. V., the

3. That on the second day of November, 19—, your petitioner filed his appeal from the judicial act or decision of the Register of Wills in admitting the said alleged will to probate, and duly entered the security required by the Act of Assembly, and the record of the proceedings before the Register has been duly certified by him and filed in this Court. 

4. Your petitioner verily believes, and expects to be able to prove that the said decedent, at the time of the execution of the alleged will, was not of sound disposing mind, memory and understanding, but on the contrary, was of unsound mind, and incompetent to execute any paper requiring the exercise of discretion, mind, memory or understanding, and that the execution of the said alleged will was procured by the contrivance and undue influence of the said F. V., one of the executors therein named, and of others whom your petitioner is at this time unable to name with precision. The facts and circumstances upon which your petitioner bases his belief are as follows: 

The decedent was upwards of seventy-nine years of age at the time of the date of the execution of the said alleged will, and was suffering from arterio sclerosis, and chronic nephritis. He was eccentric to a degree indicating unsoundness of mind. Up to the date of his death, the relations between him and your petitioner and his other nephews and nieces were pleasant, and he had

DECEDENTS' ESTATES 

intimated that it was his intention to leave his estate, or at least a large portion of it to them. I am informed that the value of his estate is upwards of two hundred thousand dollars ($200,000). By the paper which has been admitted to probate as his will, he gives to various relations legacies aggregating ten thousand dollars ($10,000) to various charities, legacies aggregating eighteen thousand dollars, ($18,000), and the entire residue of his estate to the Society. H. S., G. S. and F. V., who are the executors named in the will, are all members of the said Society, and the said F. V., for a number of years prior to the decedent's death and at the time of the execution of the alleged will, had entire charge of the decedent's affairs.

W., among whom it is provided by the said alleged will that the sum of two thousand dollars shall be equally divided.

10. Precept to Common Pleas

THE COMMONWEALTH OF PENNSYLVANIA 

SS:

To the Judges of the Court of Common Pleas of the said 

County, Greeting: 

day of 

Whereas, A. B., on the -, in the year, et cetera, presented to G. H., our Register of Wills of said county, for probate, a certain writing hereto annexed, purporting to have been made the 9 day of in the year, et cetera (or otherwise describing the paper in question), which said writing the said A. B. avers is the last will and testament of the said C. D.; and whereas, E. D., who is a son and heir of the said C. D. (or intermarried with F. D., who is a daughter and heir, et cetera, according to the fact), hath objected before our said Register that the said writing was procured by duress and constraint (stating the matters of fact objected); and

Whereas, our said register hath admitted (or refused to admit) said writing to probate as the last will and testament of the said C. D.; and whereas, the said E. D. hath appealed from the decree of our said register to our Orphans' Court for the said county (or, as the case may be): and 

Whereas, the said E. D. (or A. B.) hath requested that an issue may be directed into our said Court of Common Pleas, to try by a jury the validity of the said writing,

LETTERS TESTAMENTARY 

897 and the matters of fact which may be objected thereto in our said court:

Therefore, we command you that you cause an action to be entered upon the records of our said court, as of the day of the delivery of this our precept into the office of the prothonotary of our said court, between the said A. B. and the said E. D., so that an issue therein may be formed upon the merits of the controversy between the said parties, and tried in due course according to the practice of our said courts in actions commenced by writ: 

Further, that you cause all other persons who may be interested in the estate of the said C. D., as heirs, relations, or next of kin, devisees, legatees, or executors, to be warned, so that they may come into our said court and become party to the said action, if they shall see cause; and that you certify the result of the trial, so had in the premises, into our said Orphans' Court. Attest: 

President Judge of the Orphans' Court of the said county.

WHEREAS, We deem it expedient to send said issue to our court of common pleas for the trial of facts by jury; therefore 

WE COMMAND You that you cause an action to be entered upon the records of our said court of common pleas, as of the day of the delivery of this our precept into the office of the prothonotary of our said court, between John Smith as plaintiff, and John Jones, executor of the last will and testament of John Doe, deceased, as defendant, so that an issue therein may be formed upon the merits of the controversy between the said parties, and tried in due course according to the practice of our said courts in actions commenced by writ, to determine the following question of fact:

Is the signature to the original note, a copy of which herein appears, the genuine signature of John Doe, deceased?

O. SALES UNDER THE  1. Requirements of the Petition 

(See the Act of 1917, P. L. 388.)

The Technical details incident to the preparation of the petition are also in many counties regulated by rule of court. 

In practically every jurisdiction the following matters are required in the petition: (1) Recital of the party petitioning showing his interest in the estate, how acquired, and the jurisdiction of the court. (2) Recital of the provisions of the will (if any) relating to the property, a complete copy of the will being annexed as an exhibit. (3) Description of the property in detail with recital of title into the decedent. (4) Recital of all parties in interest with their status (as to minority, etc.) and the nature of their interests. (5) If a private sale a recital as to the terms of the sale and the party vendee. (6) Averment that the proposed sale will be to the interest and advantage of the estate. (7) Statement of valuation verified usually by affidavits of at least two real estate experts not interested in the transaction, annexed as exhibits.

(8) A showing as to officially assessed valuation accompanied by a certificate from the proper authority annexed as an exhibit. (9) Statement where necessary giving the facts as to the physical condition of the property and why the proposed sale will benefit the estate. (10) Statement as to joinder of parties and their agreement that the sale is advantageous. (11) Statement as to the reason for invoking the jurisdiction of the court, the relief desired, and the effect of the sale in the language of the statute. (12) Prayer for leave to sell or mortgage, etc., as the case may be, carefully drawn to follow as closely as possible the language of the decree. (13) Signature and affidavit by petitioner. (14) Joinder by all parties in interest, minors, by guardians, lunatics, etc., by committees, etc. (15) Exhibits as above set forth. (16) A form of decree which should be carefully drawn and should follow as closely as possible the language of the prayer of the petition.

Certain of the above requirements will of course be omitted where the sale is to be a public one. 

Where all parties do not join the prayer will be for a citation on those not concurring to show cause why the sale or mortgage should not be allowed or confirmed as the case may be. 

The provisions of the act herein before set forth-apply alike to public and private sales, though the latter are much the more numerous.

But if they shall be of the opinion that the premises aforesaid, with the appurtenances, cannot be parted and divided so as to accommodate more than one of them, that then they value and appraise the same, with the appurtenances, according to law, and make report to the next Orphans' Court after they shall have so parted or valued the same.

The Act of June 18, 1923, P. L. 840, gives Courts of record within their respective jurisdictions, power to declare rights, status, and other legal relations whether or not further relief

DECLARATORY JUDGMENTS 

1123 is or could be claimed. No action or proceeding shall be open to objection on the ground that a declaratory judgment or decree is prayed for. The declaration may be either affirmative or negative in form and effect, and such declarations shall have the force and effect of a final judgment or decree. 

Any person interested under a deed, will, written contract or other writing, constituting a contract, or whose rights, status, or other legal relations, are affected by a statute, municipal ordinance, contract or franchise, may have determined any question of construction or validity arising thereunder, and obtain a declaration of rights, status, or other legal relations thereunder. See 284 Pa. 255.

DEEDS AND RECITALS SEE ACKNOWLEDGMENTS;  

A DEED is a writing or instrument, under seal, containing some contract or agreement, and which has been delivered by the parties. In its more confined sense, it is a writing by which lands, tenements, and hereditaments are conveyed, which writing is sealed and delivered by the parties.

In some deeds covenants are inserted to oblige the parties, or one of them, to do something beneficial to, or to abstain from something, which, if done, might be prejudicial to the other. 

The following are essentials in making a deed, viz: 1st. It must be written or printed on parchment or paper. Typewriting is valid. Act 18 June, 1895, 4 Purd. 4969. 2d. The parties. must be properly qualified. 3d. There must be a proper subjectmatter, which is the object of the grant. 4th. A sufficient consideration. 5th. An agreement properly set forth. 6th. It must have been read to the party executing it, if desired. 7th. It must be signed and sealed. 8th. It must be delivered; and 9th, attested by witnesses. Subscribing witnesses are not essential. 

10th. It should be properly acknowledged before a competent officer; and 11th, it ought to be recorded upon delivery. 

A deed may be avoided, 1st. By alterations made in it after its execution. 2d. By the disagreement of those parties whose concurrence is necessary. 3d. By the judgment of a competent tribunal. 

A written scroll enclosing the word "seal," or "L. S.," is a good and valid seal in Pennsylvania. See Lorah v. Nisley, 156 

Pa. 329.

The consideration for the execution of a deed, which, as above stated, must be sufficient, may be either a good or a valuable one. A good considération is such as that of blood, or natural love and affection, as when a man grants an estate to a near relation being founded on motives of generosity, prudence, or natural duty. A valuable consideration is such as money, marriage, or the like, which the law esteems an equivalent given for the grant, and is therefore founded in motives of justice. Deeds made upon good consideration only, are considered as merely voluntary, and are frequently set aside in favor of creditors and bona fide purchasers.

If the grantor has a wife, she must sign and acknowledge the deed; otherwise she may, after the death of her husband, claim her dower, during her natural life. 

By the Act of 8 June, 1893, 3 Purd. 2449, a married woman may acquire and dispose of her property as if she were unmarried; but she may not convey or mortgage her real estate unless her husband join. Under the Act of 1 April, 1909, 5

Purd. 5393, separate acknowledgment by a wife is no longer necessary.

By the Act of 3 June, 1911, P. L. 631, Purd. (1911) 372, a married woman may convey her real estate to her husband. 

If there be interlineations or erasures in a deed, there should be a note made of them, which should be witnessed by the witnesses.

A Warranty Deed is so called, because in such deeds the grantor covenants or undertakes to insure and defend such lands and tenements from such person and to the extent therein specified. The warranty may be general or special. It is general when it warrants against all persons, and special when it warrants only against the grantor, his heirs, and those claiming under him. The old rule was, in case the grantee having a warranty deed should be evicted, in case of eviction by title paramount, that the warrantor should give him lands of equal value; in lieu of that, the consideration money and interest are now recovered; and covenants may be inserted in a deed to make the grantor liable to a still greater extent. 

Deeds by Executors, Administrators, or Guardians, are made in an official capacity, either by powers conferred by a will, or by an order of the Orphans' Court.

A Quitclaim Deed is a release or acquittal of a person's interest, whatever that may be, from all claims which the releasor has against the land therein specified.

A Deed Poll or a Single Deed is much like a Quitclaim Deed, being made by one party only (e. g., a Sheriff's Deed). It was not indented, but polled or shaved quite even; hence its name. 

Purchasers at a judicial sale should investigate the title of property so sold, since the title conveyed can only be to the extent of the interest of the party whose interest is thus sold, excepting in sales for unpaid taxes, which always bar an adverse title.

WARRANTY DEED 

1133 Deeds in Trust are given to persons to hold in fee simple, or otherwise, for the use of some other person or persons. The person holding the title is called the Trustee. The estate so held is not subject to the judgment debts of the trustee, to the dower of his wife, or the curtesy of the husband of a female trustee. 

The one for whose use the trust is created is entitled to proceeds, profits, or use.

2d. The habendum, in the form just referred to, comprised in that portion extending from (1) to (2), which is a statement of what estate or interest is granted by the deed.

26. Deed of Trust for the Sole and Separate Use of a Married Woman 

(A separate use trust can be created only for a woman married or in contemplation of immediate marriage. The deed is usually made to a trustee for the sole and separate use of the wife. However, it is not the less a separate use estate because the deed is made directly to the wife. 

If no trustee be named, equity will raise one to effectuate the grantor's intention. A clear intention to establish a sole and separate use trust must appear.

The wife's power over the sole and separate use property depends entirely upon the terms of the instrument. A separate use trust gives a wife the power to convey and mortgage, through the trustee, property without the joinder of her husband, free and clear of curtesy.) (Use same form as number one and add following after the habendum clause:)

In Trust, nevertheless, for the sole and separate use of my daughter Catharine wife of Charles

her heirs and assigns forever, free and discharged from any and all control of her said husband and of any curtesy or other interest therein on his part, with power to the said trustee to manage, let and demise the said premises hereby granted and conveyed, to receive and collect the rents and profits therefrom, and after payment of all charges thereon, to pay over the net income to the said Catharine or to such person as she shall, in writing appoint; and with further power to said. -, trustee to sell and convey, in fee simple, the whole or any part of the aforesaid premises, to any person or persons, and for such sum or sums of money as the said Catharine by writ- ing under her hand and seal, and duly acknowledged at anytime during her lifetime, or by her last will and testament, may appoint and direct.

29. Spendthrift Trust Deed 

(A peculiar feature of the Pennsylvania law of trusts is the doctrine by which an estate for life can be made nontransferable and free from the owner's debts. The trust must be an active one. The instrument

TRUSTS 

1173 creating such an estate must name a trustee (267 Pa. 207). A spendthrift trust cannot be created by a grantor for himself (218 Pa. 207).) (Use same form as number one and add following after the habendum clause):

IN TRUST, however, to collect and receive the rents, income and profits from the said premises and after paying therefrom and thereon the taxes, water rents, costs of repairs and all other necessary charges, including a commission of 5% to the trustee, to apply so much of the net income as in the judgment of the trustee shall be proper to the support and maintainence of John Doe, so long as he may live, free and discharged from liability to execution or attachment in any form for any debts or liabilities whatsoever of said John Doe or to assignment or anticipation in any manner by the said John Doe and upon the further trust, upon the death of said John Doe to convey said premises and the funds in possession of said trustee to such person or persons as the said John Doe by his last will and testament in writing duly executed shall appoint, and in default of such appointment the trustee shall convey said premises and whatever funds which may then remain in the said trust to the person or persons entitled to receive the same under the intestate laws of the state of Pennsylvania, as if the said John Doe had died seized thereof in fee.

42. Recitals to Be Used in Deeds, etc.

A RECITAL is the petetition of some former writing, or the statement of something which has been done. Touchst. 76. 

Recitals are used to explain those matters of fact which are necessary to make the transaction intelligible. 2 Bl. Com. 298. 

Thus, in a deed, it is frequently necessary to recite certain mat-

ters connected with the title, for the purpose of explaining its derivation.

DEPOSITIONS, COMMISSIONS AND LETTERS ROGATORY 

A DEPOSITION is the testimony of a witness reduced to writing in due form of law, taken by virtue of a commission or other authority of a competent tribunal. 

Rules of court generally provide that either party may at any time enter a rule to take the depositions of witnesses, upon reasonable notice to the opposite party. 

The rule to take testimony of aged, infirm or going witnesses is usually entered of course; in other cases generally a rule to show cause is required. 

By provision of the Act of 25 June, 1895, P. L. 279, a twentyday rule may be taken (as of course) to take depositions of witnesses beyond the limits of the Commonwealth and within 

100 miles of the courthouse.

By an Act of Assembly of Pennsylvania of the 26th February, 1831, 2 Purd. 1488, in all cases where a deposition is to be taken upon a commission, or on a rule of court, or of a Justice of the Peace, the individual authorized to take the deposition may issue a subpoena for any witness named, and compel his attendance by attachment, or commit him to prison if he refuses to testify.

DEPOSITIONS 

1201 Where a witness resides beyond the limits of the state, a commission may be issued upon interrogatories filed. Act of 1911, P. L. 709.

A notice to take depositions should have sufficient certainty, as to time, and place, to enable the opposite party to attend without any extraordinary search. The hours between which a deposition is to be taken, must be named, and it cannot legally be taken at any other time, unless by consent of the parties, which should be made to appear. 

A deposition taken in pursuance of a rule of court cannot be read in evidence, unless it appear by the certificate of the Justice that it was taken at the time and place mentioned in the notice. 

At the time and place named in the notice, the witness, before his deposition is taken, should be sworn or affirmed to declare the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The deposition should be written by the commissioner appointed to take it, or by the witness himself, or by one not interested in the matter in dispute, who is properly authorized by the commissioner.

When a deposition is taken before a Justice on interrogatories, it is the duty of the Justice to put the interrogatories severally to the witness, and to obtain distinct answers to each. 

A deposition taken before a Justice under a rule, ought to be reduced to writing, from the mouth of the witnesses in the presence of the Justice.

A deposition should be signed by the witness and by the commissioner; when the witness cannot write, it should be so stated, and he should affix his mark or cross.

COMMISSIONS 

If a party wishes to procure the testimony of witnesses beyond the limits of the state, a rule must be taken upon interrogatories filed, and a commission for that purpose issued. Some variation exists in the rules of court relative thereto, in the several Judicial Districts of this Commonwealth. The following forms will answer for most of the Districts, and for the remainder changes can be made to suit their practice. 

Any competent person may be appointed a commissioner. 

Justices of the Peace are also empowered to issue commissions to take depositions to be read in causes depending before them. 

A Register of Wills has like power.

atories annexed to the commission. To assist you in the performance of your duties, we would respectfully make the following suggestions: 

1. Notify all witnesses of the time and place which you shall fix for their examination. 

2. As each witness is called, either of you, or a notary, in your presence, may administer the proper oath or affirmation. The interrogatories should then be propounded to the witness and his answer to each noted in full. After the interrogatories have been answered, the cross interrogatories should be propounded, and the answers likewise noted in full. 

3. It is necessary that each page of the depositions should be signed by the witness and both of the commissioners. 

4. Any documents offered in evidence should be identified by the witness, and the identification signed by him and both of the commissioners. The documents so identified should be attached to the commission. 

5. Unless otherwise instructed there should be no counsel or any other person present at the examination except the witness, the commissioners, and the officer, if any, who swears the witness and the stenographer. 

6. No questions must be asked the witnesses except those contained in the interrogatories and cross-interrogatories attached to the commission.

DEPUTATION SEE CONSTABLES; SHERIFFS DEPUTATION is the act by which a substitute or representative is appointed.

A DEPUTY is one authorized by an officer to exercise the office or right which said officer possesses, for and in place of the latter. In general, ministerial officers can appoint deputies, but where the office partakes of a judicial as well as ministerial character, although a deputation may be made for ministerial acts, one cannot be made to authorize the performance of a judicial act; thus, a sheriff cannot appoint a deputy to hold an inquisition under a writ of inquiry, though he may to serve a writ. In general, a deputy has power to do every act which his principal might do, but he cannot appoint a deputy. A deputy should always act in the name of his principal, who is liable for the deputy's acts, performed by him as such, and for the neglect of the deputy. And the deputy is liable himself, to the person injured, for his own tortious acts.

DIVORCE DIVORCE 

A DIVORCE is the dissolution of the bonds of matrimony, or the separation of husband and wife, by the judgment of a court of competent jurisdiction, or by an act of the legislature. 

Divorces are of two kinds: 1. The divorce a vinculo matrimonii, [from the bond of matrimony], which dissolves and totally severs the marriage tie; and, 2. The divorce a mensa et thoro, [from bed and board], which merely separates the parties. 

In Pennsylvania under the present Constitution of 1873, the legislature is forbidden to pass any local or special law granting divorces.

The courts, in this state, have jurisdiction in the following cases, viz: 1. Impotency at the time of contract; 2. Knowingly entering into a second marriage, in violation of the previous vow; 3. Adultery; 4. Wilful and malicious desertion and absence from the habitation of the other, without a reasonable cause, for and during the space of two years; 5. Cruel and barbarous treatment by either husband or wife, endangering the life of the other; 6. Indignities offered to the person of either husband or wife, so as to render his or her condition intolerable and life burdensome, Act of June 28, 1923, P. L. 886; 7. Consanguinity or affinity within the table established by law, which renders marriage void ab initio, if a divorce be obtained before the death of either party, Act of 1815, Sec. 5; 8. Where the marriage was obtained by fraud and has not been subsequently confirmed; 9. Where the party respondent has been convicted of any of several specified crimes and sentenced to two years' imprisonment.

Before the Act of Assembly of 26th April, 1850, it was required that the cause of divorce should have occurred within the state, and no proceeding could be commenced for wilful and malicious desertion till the full period of two years had elapsed after such desertion had taken place. By the said Act of Assembly of 1850, the law is so changed as to enable the courts to entertain jurisdiction of all causes of divorce for desertion as aforesaid or adultery, notwithstanding the parties were, at the time of the occurrence of said cause, domiciled in another state; but, as provided by previously existing laws, no such divorce

HEAD NOTE 

1221 can be granted unless the applicant therefor is a citizen of this state, and has resided herein for the term of one year. The same act also provides that either party for the cause of wilful, malicious and continued desertion from the habitation of the other, may apply, in such case, by person or libel, to the proper court, in accordance with the provisions of the several Acts of Assembly then in force, at any time not less than six months after such cause of divorce shall have taken place; but the said court cannot proceed to make a final decree, divorcing the said parties from the bonds of matrimony, until after the expiration of two years from the time at which such desertion took place. 

See cases cited 1 Purdon 1237 note (f); see also Act of 20th 

June, 1893, 1 Purd. 1236. As to other causes occurring without the jurisdiction, see Act 28 April, 1903, 1 Purd. 1237; Act 13 

April, 1911, P. L. 60, 5 Purd. 5931.

A wife may file her bill for a divorce a vinculo matrimonii, under the Act of 1815, or for a divorce a mensa et thoro and alimony, under the Act of 1817, at her election. 1 Watts 263; 

3 S. & R. 248. If any husband maliciously either abandon his family, or turn his wife out of doors, or by cruel and barbarous treatment endanger her life, or offer such indignities to her person as to render her condition intolerable or life burdensome, and thereby force her to withdraw from his house and family, the Courts of Common Pleas of the respective counties may, upon complaint and due proof thereof, made in the manner prescribed, grant the wife a divorce from bed and board, and allow her such alimony as her husband's circumstances will admit of, so as the same does not exceed the third part of the annual profit or income of his estate or of his occupation and labor, which shall continue until a reconciliation shall take place, or until the husband shall, by his petition or libel, offer to receive and cohabit with her again, and to use her as a good husband ought to do; and then, in such case, the court may either suspend the aforesaid sentence or decree, or, in case of her refusal to return under the protection of the court, discharge and annul the same, according to their discretion; and if the husband fail in performing his said offers and engagements, the former sentence or decree may be revived and enforced, and the arrears of the alimony may be ordered to be paid.

Recrimination, condonation, or connivance, are good defenses to suits for the cause of adultery. A wife or husband having

DIVORCE 

been guilty of the crime of adultery, shall not marry the person with whom the said crime was committed during the life of the former wife or husband. Act of 13th March, 1815, Sects. 7, 9, 1 Purd. 1246-7. See Act of 28 June, 1925, P. L. 886.

The rules of court are very explicit, and should be consulted at every stage of the proceeding.
