56. Petition by Husband, Respondent, to Annul Decree of Divorce from Bed and Board (Caption.) 

The petition of the above named respondent, respectfully showeth: 

That he is informed that on the day of in the year of our Lord one thousand nine hundred and this Honorable Court made a sentence or decree conformably to the prayer of the libellant above named, that your petitioner and the said libellant should be, and they accordingly were, divorced from bed and board.

Your petitioner does not deem it proper for him, at this stage of the proceeding, to deny the allegations contained in the libel, nor to dispute the justice of the sentence pronounced by this Honorable Court, grounded upon the ex parte evidence produced to them; he is informed and advised that the said sentence is absolute, and precludes contradictions on matters of fact. 

Your petitioner is well convinced that he and the libellant can live happily together hereafter, and that their doing so will be essential to the comfort, education, and morals of their young children, and he anxiously avails himself of an indulgent provision of the law, and now offers to this Honorable Court to receive and cohabit with the said libellant again, and to use her as a good husband ought to do.

The Act 8 March, 1889, amended 16 April, 1903, 2 Purd. 1304, provides that where any party, not in possession of real estate, shall have an apparent interest or title, any person in possession and claiming title may obtain a rule on the other to bring ejectment within six months or show cause why it cannot be brought, and if he fails to appear and show cause a judgment shall be entered against him, and thereafter neither he nor any one claiming under him shall bring any ejectment for the recovery of the land.

The following form of advertisement under this act sufficiently shows the form of the petition and rule.

EQUITY EQUITY 

In its most general sense we are accustomed to call that equity which, in human transactions, is founded in natural justice, in honesty and right, and which properly arises ex aequo et bono. 

But in its more limited and legal sense, a court of equity may be said to have jurisdiction in cases of rights recognized and protected by the municipal jurisprudence, where a plain, adequate, and complete remedy cannot be had in the courts of Common 

Law. 1 Story's Equity, Secs. 1a, 37. 

In the early history of the law the sense affixed to the word equity was exceedingly vague and uncertain. It was then asserted that equity was bounded by no certain limits or rules, and that it was alone controlled by conscience and natural justice. 

3 Bl. Com. 433, 440, 441. It is now well defined with limits and rules. as well a

The first settlers of Pennsylvania brought with them the whole body of the English jurisprudence (applicable to, and requisite for their wants and situations), both that which was administered in the courts of chancery and that which was the guide of the courts of law. The principles of equity, as well as those of law, flowed in upon them from the parent source; but, in their simple state of society, they found but little occasion for distinguishing the channels. So far as regarded those principles or rules of justice, our jurisprudence was not greatly defective. They were always recognized, and pervaded our system as thoroughly, perhaps, though not in the same manner, as in the English system. Rep. of Com. on the Civil Code, 183435, 5. The whole theory of that equitable jurisprudence became incorporated with our own code, and its principles circulated through all the channels of our judicial system. They were adopted by us as fully as by any of our sister states in which a regular chancery tribunal exists, and became as binding as those of the common law (2 Rawle, 252), although up to the passing of the Act of 1836, we had, for the most part, different modes of administering relief. Report, 15, 16. Equity and law became and still are convertible terms. 15 S. & R. 125; 16 id. 278, 279. The power of exercising that jurisdiction, in a limited degree, became blended with the power to administer law under the same forms. 4 S. & R. 455; 8 id. 491; 7 id. 155; 1 Binn.

HEAD NOTE 

1275 217; 16 S. & R. 278, 279. It was in consequence of this mode of administering justice that the want of separate equitable modes of procedure was sensibly felt. In order to make the commonlaw forms of procedure subservient to the purposes of equitable relief, it became necessary to resort to fictions, and accordingly fictions became, and are still, the substratum of our equity system. Before the Revolution, the means of doing justice, for the time being, were withheld from the existing tribunals; a state of things occasioned by the conflict of opinion, first, between the legislature of the province and the privy council in England, and afterwards between the proprietary or royal governors and the legislature, upon the expediency of establishing a separate chancery tribunal. Rep. of Com. Since the Revolution and the framing of the State Constitution, these wants have, from time to time, been in some measure supplied; yet, notwithstanding these defects of form were often lamented by our judges, the jurisprudence of the commonwealth continued to labor under the reproach of inability to do complete and effectual justice, until the promulgation of the Act of 1836 above referred to. 

The said Act of 16 June, 1836, 2 Purd. 1405, relating to the jurisdiction and powers of the courts, enacted that the Supreme Court and the several Courts of Common Pleas should have the jurisdiction and powers of a court of chancery, so far as relates to: 1st. The perpetuation of testimony; 2d. The obtaining of evidence from places not within the state; 3d. The care of the persons and estates of those who are non compos mentis; 4th. The control, removal, and discharge of trustees, and the appointment of trustees and the settlement of their accounts (2 Wharton, 330); 5th. The supervision and control of all corporations other than those of a municipal character, and unincorporated societies or associations, and partnerships (5 Whart. 520; 3 W. & S. 

184-193; 6 W. & S. 552); 6th. The care of trust-moneys and property, and other moneys and property made liable to the control of the said courts; and in such other cases as the said courts have heretofore possessed such jurisdiction and powers, under the constitution and laws of the commonwealth. By the 

Act of 25 April, 1850, equity powers were extended to the several courts to perpetuate testimony in cases of lost or destroyed records of any of the courts of record. The Orphans' Court has equity powers powers (for remarks upon which see "Orphans'

EQUITY 

Courts'). The Act of 16th June, 1836, provides that in every case in which any court of the Commonwealth shall exercise any of the powers of a Court of Chancery, the same shall be exercised according to the practice in equity prescribed or adopted by the Supreme Court of the United States, unless it be otherwise provided by Act of Assembly, or the same shall be altered by the Supreme Court of the Commonwealth, by general rules and regulations made and published as therein specified. It is further provided by the same act, that the Supreme Court, when sitting in banc in the City and County of Philadelphia, and the Court of Common Pleas [and District Court] for the said city and county, shall, besides the powers and jurisdiction aforesaid, have the power and jurisdiction of Courts of Chancery so far as relates to 1st. The supervision and control of partnerships, and corporations other than municipal corporations; 2d. The care of trust-moneys and property, and other moneys and property made liable to the control of the said courts; 3d. The discovery of facts material to a just determination of issues, and other questions arising or depending in the said courts; 4th. The determination of rights to property, or money claimed by two or more persons, in the hands or possession of a person claiming no right of property therein; 5th. The prevention or restraint of the commission or continuance of acts contrary to law and prejudicial to the interests of the community or the rights of individuals; 6th. The affording specific relief, when a recovery in damages would be an inadequate remedy. By the Act of 13th 

June, 1840 (P. L. 666), and by Act of 17th May, 1845 (P. L. 

158), equity jurisdiction is extended to the Supreme Court within the City and County of Philadelphia, and the Court of Common Pleas for said county, in all cases arising in said city and county, over which Courts of Chancery entertain jurisdiction on grounds of fraud, accident, mistake, account, dower, and partition, and, by Act of 10 April, 1848 (P. L. 448), in all cases for the discovery of facts in which jurisdiction is possessed by Courts of Chancery. 

The Act of 14th February, 1857, extends the equity jurisdiction to Courts of Common Pleas throughout the state, and these equity powers are confirmed by the Constitution of 1873. The present Constitution also deprives the Supreme Court of original jurisdiction in equity cases, except as therein specially provided. 

The equity jurisdiction of Courts of Common Pleas of this

HEAD NOTE 

1277 state is confirmed and enlarged as to dower and partition by Act of 7 July, 1885, P. L. 257, as to disputes between stockholders and creditors of corporations, and questions relating to the franchises and mortgages of corporations by Acts of 19 June, 1871; 5 May, 1876; 23 March, 1877; 4 May, 1893, 2 Purd. 1417-1419. 

The equity jurisdiction of the Courts of Common Pleas of this state has been extended to matters that relate to the prevention, restraint and abatement of encroachments on public sidewalks in front of residences, churches, hotels, apartment houses, or retail stores, contrary to law and prejudicial to the interest of the community. (Act of May 3, 1927, P. L. 515.) 

The Supreme Court, by virtue of its power to devise and establish new writs and form of proceedings, has adopted rules regulating equity practice, which are obligatory upon the Courts of Common Pleas. They simplify the proceedings, and render useless the verbiage of the old forms. The following forms are designed to be in accordance with the equity rules as amended.

As to equity practice in the federal courts, see the rules promulgated by the Supreme Court of the United States.

A. B., above plaintiff, brings this Bill against C. D., and complaining, says: 

1. A. B., on the day of 

A. D. 19-, was seized and possessed of a certain tract of land [description]. day of 

2. A. B., on the 

A. D. 19—, being so seized and possessed, by deed duly executed and acknowledged, and recorded in the office for recording of deeds, etc., in and for said county, in deed book granted and conveyed to C. D., the surface of tract of land [description] being the tract aforesaid. 

3. The intention of A. B. and the said C. D., parties to the said deed, at the time of making said deed, was only a conveyance by A. B. to the said C. D. of the surface of the said lot or tract therein described, reserving the coal under the said tract to said A. B., but by accident and mistake the words of the said conveyance fail to express such intention but are ambiguous and seem to convey said tract and the coal thereunder, in so far as is set forth as follows:

Instead of using in connection with the grant, the words "All that certain surface or right of soil in and to the following piece, parcel, or tract of land," thereby

EQUITY 

effecting such result as was contemplated by the said parties to the said conveyance at the time it was made, the conveyance set forth, "all that certain surface, or tenement and tract of land," thus rendering the said conveyance ambiguous and seeming to convey not only the surface but also the coal thereunder. 

4. The word "surface" in the said conveyance is interlined and although the same is noted before attestation and execution thereof this fact renders it of even less force in restricting the grant to the extent contemplated by the parties. 

5. Further, the said conveyance by omission through accident and mistake, contains no reservation, express or implied, of the said coal to A. B., which is not only contrary to the intention of the said parties to the conveyance at the time it was made but affects and lessens materially the market value of said coal by casting doubt upon the title thereto in A. B. 

WHEREFORE, A. B. prays: 

(a) That it may be ordered, adjudged and decreed by this Honorable Court that A. B. may reform and rectify his said deed to the said C. D., bearing date the day of A. D. 19-, by cancelling the same as it now stands upon record, and executing, delivering and recording in lieu and place thereof, a similar deed to the said C. D. omitting therefrom the words "All that certain surface, messuage, tenement or tract of land," as contained in the grant of the said recited deed, and inserting in their stead, the words "All that certain surface or right of soil in and to the following piece, parcel or tract of land" in said grant, and also inserting the words "Excepting and reserving to the said A. B., his heirs and assigns, all the coal and other minerals under the said described tract of land" immediately after the said grant, and also inserting the words "Excepting and reserving as aforesaid" after the habendum, so that the said deed shall conform to the intention of the said parties thereto,

as at the time the said deed was made, and give effect thereto, and so that the same may be faithfully carried out.

ANSWER 

1. This respondent is willing to admit the truth of the facts set out in the first paragraph of the bill. 

2. This respondent admits that on 

19-, he executed a lease from G. O. to this respondent for the premises Nos. 

Street, as averred in the second paragraph of the bill; and that the complainant is assignee of the said G. O.

For greater certainty as to the terms of the said lease this respondent prays that reference may be had thereto. 

3. This respondent admits the averments contained in the third paragraph of the bill. 

4. This respondent admits that during his occupancy under the said lease he has placed in said premises certain electric wiring and switchboards or panels; an auxiliary centrifugal motor driven pump; and an extra armature for a freight elevator motor; but denies, for the reasons hereinafter set forth, that said articles are in the nature of alterations, additions or improvements, which, under the terms of the lease, are to become the property of the landlord or a part of the said premises. 

5. This respondent admits that he has placed in said premises, as set out in the fourth paragraph of this answer, certain electric wiring and switchboards or panels; an auxiliary centrifugal motor driven pump; and an extra armature, which was constructed for use in connection with a freight elevator motor. 

6. This respondent admits the averments in the sixth paragraph of the bill. 

7. This respondent admits that complainant has asserted his right to retain the said articles as part of said premises and has sent the respondent the notice of 19, a copy of which is annexed to the bill. 9 He denies, for the reasons hereinafter stated, that the

EQUITY 

complainant is entitled to retain said articles as landlord of said premises under the terms of said lease, and avers that no higher rights are conferred upon the complainant by virtue of any notice which he has sent. 

8. This respondent admits that at the time of the service of the special injunction upon him in this case he was about to remove from said premises the articles hereinbefore enumerated and avers that he has the right to do so during the continuance of the lease, which does not expire until 19-.

All of said electric wiring and panels were erected in connection with respondent's presses and machinery and as a part of respondent's plant, and the respondent therefore avers that the same are not alterations, additions or improvements to the premises as contemplated by the lease, but constitute part of respondent's plant and trade fixtures which he is entitled to remove during his tenancy. 

The freight elevator upon said premises was, when leased by this respondent and still is, furnished with a motor adequate for the uses to which the elevator was to be put.

As it was essential that this respondent should be able to use the same at all times, the respondent deemed it expedient to have an additional armature constructed, so that in case the armature on the motor should be burnt out or otherwise made unfit for use, the respondent might be able promptly to replace the same. Such armature was, therefore, constructed and is stored in said premises; but it has never been used in connection with said motor and has never been in any way physically attached to the premises. No occasion for its use has ever arisen. 

This respondent, therefore, denies that said armature so stored upon said premises constitutes an alteration, addition or improvement thereto, which the complainant is entitled to retain under the provisions of the lease. 

This respondent therefore avers that he is entitled to remove all the articles claimed by the complainant in the present cause.

TRESPASS 

1371 This respondent therefore avers that he is entitled to remove all in such case made and provided, be permitted to avail himself of all matters of defense in law to the merits of the bill in his above answer set forth, of which he might have availed himself by demurrer or plea in bar, with the same force and effect as though he had filed a separate demurrer or demurrers, plea or pleas, in bar. 

10. This respondent prays to be hence dismissed with his reasonable costs in this behalf most wrongfully sustained.

The erection of the buildings and machinery of the corporation defendant was completed early in the present year, and it has already transacted a profitable and increasing business. 

If its business can be continued, in all reasonable probability, great benefits will result. If it be destroyed, and if the property be sold under executions by creditors, inequality of payment will result and great destruction of value must ensue. 

5. The corporation defendant is at the present time insolvent. If its business be broken up, it will become largely insolvent. There is imminent danger that its property, plant and machinery will be broken up, scattered and irreparably injured by separate executions and sales, instead of being kept together to be managed and sold as a whole, as it ought to be, for the equal interest and equitable protection of all concerned. A. General Form for Title of Answer 

The answer of the defendant, [or one of the defendants;] or, the joint and several answers of the defendants, [or two of the defendants,] to the bill of complaint of -, complainant.

B. Title of Answer Where There Is Only One Defendant to an Original Bill

The answer of A. B., defendant, to the bill of complaint of C. D., complainant.

C. Title of Answer Where a Defendant Is an Infant 

The answer of A. R. an infant under the age of twentyone years by her guardian, one of the defendants to the bill of complaint of J. C. and T. R., J. F. and J. L. complainants.

Puts in Her Answer to an Original and Amended Bill The answer of S. B. widow, one of the defendants to the [original and] amended bill of complaint of N. P. complainant.

T. Answer Where Defendant Requests Relief 

After fully answering the allegations of the bill, defendant may aver such additional facts, having a direct relation to any of the causes of action set forth in the bill, as he believes will entitle him to affirmative relief against plaintiff, and such other facts as may tend to invalidate an anticipated defense on plaintiff's part; and, either with or without setting forth additional facts, may pray such relief as he shall deem himself entitled to under the pleadings. To the additional facts, if any, he may require plaintiff to reply within fifteen days after service of the answer, under penalty of having an order, as of course, entered by defendant, that they be taken as admitted, with like exceptions as in the case of an answer to the bill.

ERROR CORAM VOBIS 

A writ of error directed to the same court which tried the cause, to correct an error of fact not attributable to the court, is a writ of error coram vobis. Where it issued from the king's bench, it was called the writ of error coram nobis because the king was supposed to sit there. Where infancy or coverture is a defense, and the judgment voidable for these or other reasons in fact, the writ coram vobis will issue on an allowance by the Common Pleas. On the return of the writ, the plaintiff assigns the special error in fact. If the errors are sustained, the judg ment is revocatur.

The following forms in error coram vobis are taken from Day v. Hamburgh, 1 Bro. 78. SIR: Præcipe

ERRORS AND APPEALS 

Speaking broadly, judgments of inferior courts are reviewed by appellate courts chiefly in two forms of proceedings; such as are according to the course of the common law being removed by writ of error, and those in equity or similar causes, analogous to proceedings under the civil law, by appeal or certiorai. 

In Pennsylvania, by the Act of 9th May, 1889, P. L. 158, 2 Purd. 1445, all appellate proceedings in the Supreme Court theretofore taken by writ of error, appeal, or certiorari shall be taken in a proceeding to be called an appeal; but this act does not extend the right of review or change the essence of the proceedings. Rand v. King, 134 Pa. 641; Commonwealth v. Bird, 144 Pa. 194, 25 W. N. C. 361.

As a general rule, an appeal lies only from a final judgment; but in certain cases an interlocutory judgment may be reviewed. Such are chiefly judgments in feigned issues, refusal of judgment for want of sufficient affidavit of defense, applications to open judgment (2 Purd. 1436-8), decrees granting or refusing injunctions (2 Purd. 1424-5), and decrees on bill for account, requiring the account to be taken (2 Purd. 1439). 

Until 1895, all appellate proceedings from the Courts of Common Pleas, Quarter Sessions, Oyer and Terminer, and Orphans'

Court, were taken to the Supreme Court. By Act of 24th June, 1895, P. L. 212, the Superior Court is established: and to this court appeals are to be taken in most civil causes involving an amount not exceeding $2,500, and in criminal cases, except those of felonious homicide, etc. (2 Purd. 1440 et seq.) Provisions are also made by this act for further appeal, &c. 

To supersede execution, the appeal must be taken within the periods fixed by the several Acts of Assembly on the subject. 

See 2 Purd. 1433.

The practice in the Superior Court is intended to conform as nearly as may be to that of the Supreme Court, but there are certain differences.

Forms are given herein for practice in both Courts. The general forms of paper books and of assignments of error are believed to be sufficient for either court.

See Purdon's Digest (13th Ed.), title "Errors and Appeals"; and see, Rules of Supreme and Superior Courts.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF PENNSYLVANIA 

(Caption.)

The petition of A. L. P. 

To the Honorable, the Justices of the Supreme Court of Pennsylvania:

Your petitioner respectfully represents as follows: 

1. Your petitioner was the appellant in the above case. 

2. The questions involved in the appeal were: (a) Is the bailee of a vehicle for hire responsible for the negligent driving of a friend when they are on a joint pleasure trip and the bailee is not in a position to have actual physical control over the way in which the vehicle is driven? (b) If the owner of a vehicle hires it, together with a driver, to a third person, do the control and responsibility for the management of the vehicle pass to the third person or do they remain in the bailor?

SUPERIOR TO SUPREME 

1483 (c) Can a married woman be held liable for her torts in a suit in which her husband has not been joined as codefendant? 

3. The Superior answered the first two questions in the affirmative. This is, therefore, the first recorded case in which imputed negligence has been made the basis of liability where the relation of master and servant did not exist.

The defendant hired an automobile from a public garage. It was sent out in charge of a professional chaffeur, who had positive instructions from his employer not to allow anybody else to run the car. He allowed the defendant's guest to run it, and an accident occurred. 

The Superior Court has decided that the defendant is liable in damages to those who were injured. 

4. An important principle of the law of negligence is involved. This is the first case in this State in which this point has been decided, and no reported case in any State has carried the doctrine of imputed negligence so far.

The opinion of the Superior Court is hereto attached, and copies of the paper books in the case are submitted herewith.

Your petitioner prays that this Court may allow an appeal from the Superior Court to the Supreme Court in this case, with the same effect as if originally taken thereto. 

And she will ever pray, etc. (Affidavit.)

Attention is also called to the following rule, especially so much thereof as refers to filing proof of service of notices in the court below:

Rule 58. Immediately upon taking his appeal appellant shall serve notice thereof on the opposite party or his counsel; on the stenographer who took the testimony, if the official transcript thereof has not been filed; also on the judge who made any ruling or entered any order, judgment or decree, of which appellant complains and the reasons for which do not already appear of record; and shall promptly file in the court below proof of the service of such notices. A failure to comply with this rule and promptly to serve notice on the court below, with a concise statement of the matters complained of and regarding which it is alleged the reasons therefor do not appear of record, may be considered as a waiver of all objections to the ruling, order, judgment or decree in question. On receipt of the note here required, the official stenographer shall forthwith proceed to have his notes transcribed, approved and filed, and the court below shall forthwith file of record at least a brief statement, in the form of an opinion, of the reasons for the ruling, order, judgment or decree therein referred to, or shall specify in writing the place in the record where such reasons may be found, and this opinion or writing shall be attached to the record and printed as part thereof.

34. Paper Book-(Appellee) (See Supreme and Superior Court Rule 47) 

This need not include anything but the argument, but may include a counter-statement of the questions involved, and a history of the case with the facts as appellee claims them to be. It is good practice to include an index, and the appellee may print evidence omitted from the appellant's paper book.
